Zooming in 

Below the themes and sub-themes which are most often talked about or discussed by the respondents are elaborated on and linked to theoretical notions. This ‘zooming in’ provides a closer look at the content of the victims’ narratives. It shows what the victims have experienced during the Communist regime, how they gave meaning to these experiences and how these experiences influence(d) their stories and future lives. 

Hidden Victimhood 

As told in the introduction chapter, the Afghan victims of the Communist regime received little attention throughout the years. Even though most Afghan victims have fellow sufferers in their direct social environment, the Dutch society and culture they now live in, simply do not know what has happened in Afghanistan and what it has done to the Afghan people who are currently residing in the Netherlands. Therefore it can be argued that there is no societal approval for their victimhood and this makes it hard for the respondents to share their story with their social environments, which in turn impedes processing their trauma. The unfamiliarity with their victimhood, the suffering it entailed an still entails, make their victimhood hidden. This first theme appeared to be the most important theme within the victims’ narratives and contains the following subthemes: recognition of the victimhood, suffering and trauma. 

Recognition of the Victimhood 

What can be learned from the Afghan history, is that there is not much known about the committed atrocities during the Communist regime in Afghanistan and the victimisation experiences of the people. As shortly pointed out in the introduction chapter, the Afghan victims feel like research is mostly done on the offenders, and not so much on the victims. 

‘’You are actually the first researcher who pays attention to the side of the Afghan victims, so far there were only three or four researches to the side of the offenders.’’ Aamir 

During the interviews it became clear that the unawareness and incomprehensibility are very painful and frustrating for the respondents. 40 

‘’ I think this is a very deep issue. You know, a lot of research is busy writing about criminals, think about the Apartheid crimes and the Rwanda crimes. But when you look at Afghanistan… Since 1978 until now there is violence, human rights violations and systematic crimes. We have to explain, we have to tell people about these crimes and what it has brought to the people of Afghanistan. Therefore I am always busy writing, because it is now really known.’’ Aamir 

And while their willingness to talk about their experiences was immensely high, this does not imply that it was easy for them to tell their story. Many respondents noticed that telling their stories would bring back memories and that it was emotional for them to go through these painful memories. Most respondents told their story for the very first time to an outsider and they felt proud and honoured by the fact that there was finally someone who actually wanted to hear their stories. 

‘’I feel honoured to tell my story to you. I am honoured that you want to write about Afghanistan and that you might publish it. It feels like the voice of the people, who are already forgotten, are finally going to be heard.‘’ Taleeb 

This is also confirmed by Malik as the statement below shows. 

‘’I thank you, I thank you for choosing me and my country for your research. Afghanistan is tormented by wars. It means a lot to me that you have chosen my country Afghanistan.’’ Malik 

The fact that many respondents told their life stories for the first time is striking to notice. With the eye on the victims’ desire to be understood and acknowledged by others, it is important for them to share their stories. The statement below shows how special the experience of telling the life story was. 

> ‘’

Today was a good day. While I was working, I thought: today I am happy. There is this girl who is writing her thesis and she is interested in my story. Of course she is doing it for her own thesis, but at the same time she does something meaningful to me.’’ Elias 

By means of telling their life narratives, the victims are able to connect it with that of their direct social environment and with their more distant social representations of the community, 41 

including the justice system (Pemberton, Aarten & Mulder, forthcoming). Current research seems to play an important part here. That means, by cooperating in this research and telling their personal story to the researcher, the first effort to build bridges between the Afghan victims and the Dutch society is made. In the long term, this can contribute to a connection and mutual understanding between both groups. 

All valuable things the Afghan victims built up back in Afghanistan, such as education, housing or friends and family, were gone the moment they arrived in the Netherlands. The sense of communion they felt in Afghanistan, was gone. Where they once had a close connection to their home country, they were forced to leave this close connection and find a new connection in the Netherlands. This was difficult for them because they did not know the country, the language, its people and so on. They simply had no bond, no sense of communion, with the Netherlands. In addition, the fact that the Dutch society is unaware of the victimhood of their Afghan citizens, does not create a feeling of acknowledgement and does not invite the Afghan victims to share their stories, which in turn pushes them further away from the Dutch society. However, sharing your (life) story helps rebuilding your sense of communion (Pemberton, Aarten & Mulder, forthcoming). This makes the importance of current research clear. In order to reduce the gap between the Afghan victims and the Dutch society, the victims’ narratives need to be under attention. 

Suffering 

In view of the life stories and the suffering it entails, it is understandable that the respondents have the desire to be heard. As a result of all the emotional and physical torture practices during their time in prison, the respondents were constantly suffering in one way or another. In contrast to other chapters of their lives, respondents were able to tell about their suffering in great detail. The respondents knew exactly which day they were captured, how the arrest went, how they were brought to the investigation place and what happened next. Also the torture practices were explained exhaustively and the respondents knew exactly what had been said during tortures and which members of the KhAD were present. However, during the interviews it was remarkable that the respondents were not extensive in telling stories about, for example, their youth. 

I: ‘’So, if we look at the beginning of your life story, your youth…’’ Respondent interrupts: ‘’Yes, maybe I can start with the coup d’état, that was in 1978. That is where it all began.’’ Nabil 42 

Most respondents felt the urge to immediately shift to the episode of the victimisation. This is in coherence with the literature which stresses that especially negative life events are at the core of life stories (Pemberton, 2015). 

The lives of the respondents back in Afghanistan during the Communist regime were regulated by fear and anxiety and some respondents are still scared today. All respondents are ex-political prisoners and stayed in prison for a certain amount of time. As can be read in the historical framework, the circumstances in Sedarat (the investigation place) and Pul-E-Charkhi (the central prison) were grievous. This is confirmed by all the respondents. They all experienced physical torture practices like beatings, being forced to stand for an infinite period of time, sleep deprivation, tearing out of hair and fingernails, electric shocks, and so on. 

‘’I stood there for three days and three nights. It was in a big hallway. There were moments I fell down because I could not stand anymore. But then the armed soldier came, hit you, and forced you to stand up again.’’ Habib 

Emotional torture was also part of the ordinary state of affairs, for example cursing, offending or manipulating. What became clear from the interviews is that the humiliating character of these torture practices was more harmful than the actual torture and suffering itself. 

‘’The guards were extremely brutal. They were in power to decide about your faith: life or death. They were allowed to mistreat you in all possible ways. They often cursed or said: ‘’Walk faster, not that fast, walk slowly, not that slowly, do not look at me.’’ All those kinds of stupid things. They were actually bullying.’’ Sabir 

The humiliating character of the torture practices can also be seen in the way they punished people. They treated people in an inhumane way, almost as if these prisoners were animals. This was extremely painful and embarrassing for the respondents. During the interviews it is noticed that talking about these humiliating experiences in particular is very difficult. 

‘’There was this garden… I was forced to stand there in the middle of the night while it was snowing. It was extremely cold; my whole body shivered and I was half naked. I was completely wet and I did not know what was actually happening to me. I fell down and I was not able to move anymore, but they forced me to stand. Then I fell again. Two guards brought me inside and coerced me again to stand on just one foot while they were beating me.’’ Habib 43 

The process of dehumanisation has many consequences for victims. Dehumanisation goes hand in hand with social ostracism, which undermines the victim’s sense of belonging, control, self-esteem, meaningfulness and self-regulation (Bastian & Haslam, 2010). In other words, treating people in a dehumanising way will undermine or reduce their sense of agency. Dehumanisation also entails moral disengagement: the process whereby people are placed outside the moral circle, which is why certain rights, standards and conducts are deprived from these people. This disconnection from the wider community is a central aspect of treating people as less than a human being (Bastian & Haslam, 2010). Putting it like this, approaching people in a dehumanising way might also affect the victim’s sense of communion. Feeling less than a human being stands in the way of the sense of belongingness to other people (Bastian & Haslam, 2010). The victims’ sense of communion with the own social environment, e.g. friends and family, was already deprived the moment they went to prison. On top of that, the armed soldiers also tried to cut off the victims’ last sense of communion by means of their actions; their sense of communion with their co-prisoners or fellow sufferers. The most obvious example is that many respondents have spent a longer period of time in isolation. They were literally placed outside the moral circle. 

‘’They pushed me into a small room and they closed the door. For two days, they left me there in complete darkness without seeing anyone. The only thing I heard were footsteps.’’ Habib 

The respondents experienced their time in isolation as horrific and preferred being in a prison cell with others. 

‘’I was there with 3000 people within one room, but it felt like a relief. It was better than the isolation.’’ Nabil 

In this sense, the humiliating torture practices in prison undermined both their sense of agency and communion. 

What stands out from the narratives is that their own suffering is considered as less harmful than watching other prisoners suffer. Sometimes the prisoners needed to watch the torture of co-prisoners under the guise of: ‘’If you do not talk, this is what will happen to you.’’ 

From time to time prisoners were even forced to watch a family member or dear friend being tortured. Remarkably, several respondents spoke about the so called ‘execution nights’ as their most painful memory. 

‘’Anti-revolutionaries who were condemned to execution were brought to my prison cell. I got to know these people in a couple of days and I got used to them. Then at one night, guards came 44 

into our cell and started to call their names out loud. They were deported to the execution place and I never saw them again. […] If I have nightmares, it is always about execution night.’’ 

> Ghulam

The suffering of the respondents and the humiliating character of the prison regime in general appeared to have affected both the sense of agency and the sense of communion. Agency is, among other things, important for an individual’s self-esteem, self-respect and self-control. The experience of severe victimisation calls into question all these competences. 

‘’The enduring insecurity, not knowing what was going to happen next. That was extremely stressful and exhausting.’’ Wahid. 

By treating the prisoners in such a horrific and humiliating manner, they actually took the agency of the respondents away. During their time in prison, the respondents were by no means capable of controlling their environment; everything they said or did was commissioned by the regime. The statement below shows by what means the prisoners’ self-control was deprived. 

‘’Prisoners were tied to some sort of beds. Subsequently they received electric shocks. Well as you might understand, that was one hell of a party. They were not able to hold back their defecation, so the whole room was full of blood, defecation and other substances. That was horrible.’’ Adeib 

The statement has a painful ironic undertone, ‘’ one hell of a party’’, which can be explained by the fact that the regime took over every single aspect of life, even basic human things like defecation. There was no self-control at all and their self-esteem and self-respect was completely taken away by means of torture practices as described above. When we look at the sense of communion and how this is affected during their time in prison, two things can be distinguished. First of all, the respondents felt a sense of communion with the Afghan community they used to live in and they shared norms and values with this community. The experience of victimisation calls into question these norms and values. As mentioned before, this sense of communion is already disrupted the moment they enter prison; the bonds with their community were literally cut off. However, the sense of communion becomes even more affected in case the offender was part of the same Afghan community. As the following statement shows, this was also the case for the Afghan victims. 

‘’They started to torture me. Especially the man I knew from the law faculty was harsh on me. I knew him and he knew me and he told me: ‘’I know you! Do you know me? I see you became 45 

fat, are you that happy with your anti-revolutionary activities?’’ Yes, especially he tortured me multiple times, he was really known at the faculty.’’ Ghulam 

The fact that they once felt a sense of belongingness with the person who is now torturing them, for example an ex-fellow student, disturbed their norms and values. In fact, they shared a morality with the person who immensely contributes to their experience of victimisation. Ultimately, this have led to the undermining of their sense of communion with their former community . Secondly, in order to survive, it seemed necessary for the victims to establish a new sense of communion within prison. Suffering together seemed to be better than suffering alone. 

‘’I was there with 3000 people within one room, but it felt like a relief. It was better than the isolation. We knew each other, we were together, everyone was scared. […] You were able to talk to people. We suffered from the same pain, we had the same destiny. We shared everything.’’ Nabil 

As can be seen in the above quotation of Nabil, the respondents valued the contact they had with fellow prisoners. The desire to closely relate to and cooperate with others is embedded in human nature (Diehl, Owen & Youngblade, 2014) and with an eye on this notion it is sequacious that the prisoners tried to connect with each other and took care of each other, which can be seen in the statement below. 

‘’I suffered from severe asthma, but I was brought to a prison cell where other prisoners were smoking. It was horrible, I wished I could go back to my isolation cell. But the people within my cell tried to take care of me and spare me. There was this tiny puncture in the door and the prisoners used this puncture to smoke through. Even though it was not that effective, they really tried to help me.’’ Ghulam 

Although it is probably not possible to fully re-establish the sense of communion in a prison environment, a sense of care, help and belongingness, and thus a sense of communion, can be noticed. So far, it is discussed what the suffering of the victims in prison entailed and how this has affected their existence at that time. However, the suffering has also influenced broader concepts of the life story, namely the present and the future. Forms of severe victimisation and suffering the way the Afghan victims did, often cause shattered assumptions about life, which means that their perceptions of the world as a virtuous and safe place have changed. Before the Communist regime came to power, the respondents felt safe within their home country. 46 

‘’We had a good and calm life, there were no concerns or problems. […] It all went well until the regime came to power, then the problems started. I did not know what they were capable of, I was not known with politics, but they killed my brother.’’ Elias 

As can be seen in the statement above, this feeling of safety within Afghanistan completely disappeared. It is noteworthy that the feeling of safety among the respondents never returned, which made them ultimately move to the Netherlands. The victimisation disrupted their perception of the world as a safe place. There are respondents who, until today, do not feel safe in the Netherlands because of the presence of people with 1F status: ‘’My torturer is in the Netherlands, actually a lot of them are.’’ Aamir In addition to that, many respondents are still afraid to go back to Afghanistan. 

‘’R: Nowadays, if I visit Kabul, I am still scared. The security force is still the same as during the regime, there is no change. I: You are still scared? R: Yes, I am still scared. I am truly scared. I know these people and I know what I have been through. And they are still in Kabul.’’ Hakim 

When talking about shattered assumptions in combination with the concept of agency, which is an important aspect of the self, something interesting stands out. What became clear from the interviews is that status and achievement with regards to education and a job, are very important for the respondents. This could be noticed by the manner in which all respondents repeatedly spoke about their studies and jobs back in Afghanistan. 

‘’I was always one of the best students, I had a special diploma. It was a red diploma with golden ornaments. After my studies, I was able to work as a professor at the University of Kabul.’’ Kabir 

In Afghanistan, they were all highly educated and they fulfilled high positions. From the way they talked about their achievements, it could be argued that the competences the self possessed, made them very confident and proud. As elaborated above, this strong sense of agency is dismissed or at least affected by the prison regime. What is interesting to see, is what happened to their sense of agency after the victimisation. Due to this experience, for some respondents there seems to be a discrepancy between the self before the regime, that is the self with a certain status and achievement-oriented, and the self after the regime. 47 

‘’When I came to the Netherlands, I just wanted to continue my job, my career. But the diplomas I achieved back in Afghanistan had less value in the Netherlands. I was not even able to have a job with my Afghan diplomas.’’ Nabil 

What becomes clear from the statement mentioned below, is that agency elements of the self such as status, achievement and respect are still important for the respondent, but these agency aspects are not at all or to a lesser extent present due to their victimisation experience. 

‘’One of the biggest differences is the Dutch culture and society. […] Back in Afghanistan I received much status and respect, I had a good life. Everyone knew me and I really had a voice. However, when we came here, I had to start from scratch, which was extremely difficult. Until today I am not able to fulfill my job as professor.’’ Taleeb 

It feels like they lost a major part of their agency, which is hard to re-establish with an eye on the language barrier and their physical and mental health complaints. The present and future self, that means the self after their time in prison and after the regime, is no longer perceived as one with status and as achievement-oriented. 

Trauma 

As might be obvious, the suffering of the respondents is not limited to their time in prison. The interviews made clear that all respondents have not yet fully processed the events. Some suffering turned into serious and chronic complaints or a trauma for life. These complaints are emotional and/or physical. A few respondents did mention to have physical complaints such as suffering from asthma, backache or chronic pain in other parts of their body. But above all, the experiences in Afghanistan affected the respondents mentally. ‘’I believe you are marked for life after such an experience. I will never become a normal person.’’ Sabir Mental health issues that are most often referred to are restlessness, flashbacks, nightmares or other sleeping problems and depression. Most respondents suffer from such mental health issues on a daily basis. In some cases, medical treatment is still necessary in order to deal with these mental health problems. 

‘’Some memories are too painful to talk about. Therefore I am under medical treatment since 18 years. I take medication on a daily basis and once a month I visit my doctor.’’ Aamir 

What can also be noticed is that the suffering of the respondents affects them not only on a personal level; the experiences in Afghanistan affect other aspects of life as well. For example, many respondents suffer from the inability to enjoy the pleasant things in life. 48 

‘’It is really hard for me to enjoy things in life and this can be tedious for my family as well. They often say to me: ‘‘You do not enjoy it at all!’’ I do try to relish, but sometimes I am just not able to do that. My priority is to make my family, my children, happy. I want them to enjoy life and that they are not lacking anything. I do not want them to experience the same things as I have experienced.’’ Nabil 

Most respondents have experienced the Communist regime accompanied by their wives, and sometimes even by their children. Other respondents got married afterwards. In both cases, the victimisation experiences often have an effect on the family life. 

‘’I did not see my daughter the first two and a half years of her life. […] A bond between father and daughter needs to develop from birth, but I missed these very important years. It affected us both. I feel guilty towards my daughter, she missed the love of a father in the early years of her life. […] I told you I could not enjoy things in life, but I see the same patterns in the lives of my wife and daughter.’’ Ghulam 

The quotation above shows that the life trauma is not limited to the victims themselves. The victimhood of the Afghan victims and all the suffering it entails, affect the victims’ lives and the people around them in many different ways. 

The Greater Good 

As elaborated in the first theme, all respondents suffered from different kinds of torture practices during the regime and the consequences of these practices are noticeable until today. However, what is interesting to see, is that the victimhood of most respondents is characterised by self-sacrifice in order to offer resistance to the regime. The respondents stood up against the regime in order to accomplish a higher goal: freedom and independency for Afghanistan and its people. This aim seemed to be kept in mind from the first moment the Communist Regime came to power. This can be seen in the involvement in (student) resistance movements of most respondents. 

‘’At a certain point you have to make decisions. My country was occupied and ruled by the Soviets. Then you want to stand up for your country. Stand up for the independency of your own country, for freedom. We thought: someone has to sacrifice. If you do not sacrifice, others cannot benefit. You have to make choices.’’ Nabil 

The way the respondents handled investigation can also be related to self-sacrifice. The respondents chose deliberately not to answer the investigatory questions in order to minimise 49 

the amount of people captured. However, this choice was a risky one because they knew this refusal could have negative consequences, for example: severe torture practices during next interrogations. But despite everything, they refused to answer and that is where the self-sacrifice is detectable. The self-sacrifice can also be seen in light of the concept of agency. As explained extensively above, the treatment in prison was intended to deprive the prisoners of their agency. By consciously refusing to answer questions and withholding information, the prisoners retained a bit of self-control and at the same time this may have given them a feeling of power in the face of their abusers. 

‘’If you fight together, you feel stronger. […] It feels good, it gives you a sense of pride. You belong to something meaningful, you belong to the people who sacrifice themselves. […] It becomes a risky game between interrogator and prisoner: who is stronger? Is the interrogator able to obtain useful information? It is a game that is played with your life.’’ Sabir 

As can be seen in the above quotation, the choice to self-sacrifice and to not betray friends, family or confederates has some communal aspects as well. Being together in the resistance against the regime gave the respondents a feeling of communion, conjunction and friendship. By not telling the interrogators who is with you, you are helping each other and this creates an interrelationship between the prisoners. These feelings are an important motivation to not betray confederates and stay strong. 

‘’They wanted to have information about my friends. Who was against the regime? Who was our leader? That kind of information. Betrayal. But why would you provide information about the people who are fighting for freedom and independency and who are willing to sacrifice?’’ 

> Nabil

The actions of self-sacrifice in the past seem to still have an influence until today. It helps the respondents to put their own actions and thoughts in perspective and it gives them the feeling that they did something meaningful even though they were in prison. As can be read in the below mentioned quotation, striving for the greater good gives a feeling of pride as well. 

‘’It is a dark and dangerous experience, but for me… It is very nice because they captured me for freedom, social justice. I am proud. […] I am always explaining to my daughters: you have to be proud! I was in prison for twelve years, but not because I was a thief, but because I was an intellectual who was striving against the Soviet occupation. So for this reason I am proud.’’ 

> Aamir 50

This proud feeling might improve the sense of agency in the long run. By giving the victimhood and suffering a valuable meaning, as the statement above shows, the chances are that victims will not just remain in their suffering. It gives them a feeling of achievement and responsibility within their victimhood and this will benefit the self-esteem in the long term. 

Not Letting Go of Afghanistan 

The earlier themes make it evident that the past of the Afghan victims is still chasing them. All the events they have experienced still dominate their daily lives. Additionally, the country Afghanistan itself is also of major importance to the victims. This leads to the third theme: ‘Not Letting Go of Afghanistan’. This third theme consists of two sub-themes: holding on to the past and moving towards the future. 

Holding on to the past 

The nostalgia towards the country Afghanistan itself is a reason why the past still dominates the respondents’ lives. Due to cultural differences between Afghanistan and the Netherlands, and their close connection to their home country, the respondents do not seem to be able to live fully in the present. During the interviews it felt like several respondents were with their hearts still in Afghanistan and in the past. This can be perceived by how they talked about the ‘’ beautiful country of Afghanistan and its wonderful people’’ , and also by the manner in which Afghanistan still plays a part in their daily lives. Multiple respondents noticed that their everyday thoughts are still with Afghanistan and that they remain up to date with regards to the Afghan news. 

‘’It totally dominates my life, I am always busy with Afghanistan, with the exception of family occasions or gatherings. But I am always worrying about the culture of impunity in Afghanistan and about all the offenders who are still not convicted. I regularly follow the Afghan news and sometimes my wife is saying: ‘’Why are you still watching the news of Afghanistan? It only makes you sad because there will not be any improvement soon, only deterioration.’’ But I just cannot let it go, I need to know what happens in Afghanistan and if necessary, I want to react on social media. I am involved in multiple organisations that are concerned with human rights. That is because of what I have been through.’’ Ghulam 

As a consequence, they are confronted with the dire situation in Afghanistan almost on a daily basis, which brings back memories every time, especially when they see some familiar faces appear in the news. Although they all prefer to return to Afghanistan one day and to live there 51 

for the rest of their lives, they accept the Netherlands as their second country. They are particularly grateful for the granted safety and stability within the Netherlands. 

‘’ I am still an Afghan. I learned a lot of the Dutch society and therefore I am really thankful. My choice for the Netherlands was not a mistake. Instead it has been a wonderful choice.’’ Elias 

Moving towards the future 

The lack of safety in Afghanistan and the wish for a better future is what ultimately brought them to the Netherlands, although this decision changed their lives and futures completely. All respondents have children and their main priority is to make sure that their children have future prospects in the Netherlands. Nevertheless, the respondents are not sure whether their own future should be in the Netherlands or in Afghanistan. Almost all story tellers have the desire to go back to their roots, if the situation in Afghanistan allows it. 

‘’Not only me, but also my children and wife, we are waiting for the day we can be meaningful for our home country. […] Everything we do right now is for the Netherlands, but we want to mean something for Afghanistan as well, which we are not able to do at this point.’’ Hakim 

As long as it is not safe to return to Afghanistan, many respondents stand up for the human rights violations in Afghanistan at a distance. Most of them are actively involved in organisations that support Afghan victims, or contribute to the improvement of the situation in Afghanistan. Being active in such organisations seems to serve as a coping strategy for them. 

‘’ I have a new goal in life; the improvement of human rights in Afghanistan. And I strive for justice for the victims in that period. If I can continue this job, I am processing my trauma. So I think I just keep going like this.’’ Ghulam 

Additionally, their active participation is also related to the process of sense- and meaning-making. By making something meaningful out of their suffering, they give a new meaning to their victimhood. To go even further, the active participation and their motives are reminiscent to the redemption sequence, as explained in the theoretical framework. So instead of being sad and restrained due to their suffering, the experienced events in Afghanistan motivate the respondents to take action in order to contribute something positive and meaningful. This might give them a renewed sense of agency. By doing something valuable for the country themselves, they might experience feelings of achievement and self-mastery. 

‘’ I worked with people with psychiatric complaints and the psychiatrist always said to his patients: ‘’You have to share your story with other people, that will help you.’’ […] So when 52 

the AVR Foundation was founded, I thought by myself: I am going to be a volunteer. Maybe I have limited knowledge about, for example, science, but I can share my story. I am a victim and by telling my story I help myself, but also other people around me.’’ Elias 

At the same time, the underlying motive for these actions can be based on communion aspects. The story tellers once felt connected and safe within the Afghan society and/or community. According to the interviews, this sense of communion appeared to be important for them. The respondents consider themselves Afghans in the first place and with an eye on their wish to return someday, it can be argued that their motives for active participation within organisations is meant to re-establish this feeling of communion. At the same time, helping the Afghan community together with companions might create new relationships and friendships and thus a new sense of communion. 

Wish for Justice 

It is important for victims to make sense of their victimhood. As can be read in the previous themes, some respondents tried to give sense to their victimhood, e.g. pride, in light of a higher purpose: the freedom and independency of Afghanistan and its people. Others turned their victimhood into motivation to do something meaningful for Afghanistan. The experience of severe victimisation seemed to create a sense of injustice and affected the belief in legitimate authorities, as will be shown below. Yet it now motivates them to strive for justice in order to fulfil their wish. This leads to the last theme, the ‘Wish for Justice’, including two sub-themes: sense of injustice and the disbelief in justice. 

Sense of injustice 

During the Communist regime, the Afghan victims faced many injustices. The injustice started the moment the Communist regime came to power in 1978. The people of Afghanistan were forced to follow the rules of the regime. For example, they were not allowed to listen to radio stations like the BBC. Additionally, ‘’ without any reason’’, the adherents of the regime brutally captured, tortured and murdered thousands of people. 

‘’You were not even allowed to have an opinion. You were not allowed to say things out loud. This is our country, we should own it! But we were not allowed to say it. I did not have a weapon, I had nothing, only my opinion. I was a student back then. I was against the occupation, I just did not want people to be killed. I wanted freedom of speech. I did not hurt anyone, not a single person! My opinion was enough to have me captured and tortured.’’ Nabil 53 

Above quotation is another example of injustice that almost all respondents faced. Several respondents joined nonviolent student resistance movements because they wanted to express themselves against the regime. However, being against the regime was already enough for the Afghan people to be captured. Being captured for just having an opinion turned out to be very painful and is experienced as a major injustice. As a result of all these kinds of injustice, there is a strong sense of injustice among all respondents. According to Shklar (1990) the sense of injustice in case of victims can be described as follows: ‘’The special kind of anger we feel when we are denied promised benefits and when we do not get what we believe to be our due. It is the betrayal that we experience when others disappoint expectations that they have created in us.’’ (p. 83). This sense of injustice is strongly reflected in the life narratives of the Afghan victims. As noted, nowadays the Afghan victims are still confronted with their torturers. For example, officers of the Communist regime have senior positions in the current Government of Afghanistan and some high officers fled to the Netherlands and live now ‘next to’ them. 

‘’I saw him here, just here in the Netherlands. […]. He has the Dutch nationality right now and they live in the Netherlands for years. I saw it with my own eyes. I would never forget this person.’’ Elias 

The respondents cherish the hope that the offenders, especially the ones residing in the Netherlands, will be captured one day with the help of the Dutch Government and other stakeholders. But ‘’How will these perpetrators ever be captured when no one is looking for them?’’ The quotation below is a painful illustration of their sense of injustice, it shows the frustration and anger that come along with the injustice that is inflicted on them. 

‘’How long do we have to wait and be quiet? Every month we hear that someone from the Communist Government went back to Afghanistan to become a minister or something. […] And we cannot do anything about it. They have their own court, their own power, and why? Here in the Netherlands they have their own passport! We work and live and they get money from the Government. And yet again, we cannot do anything about it. They live better than we do [laughs]. We work and get nothing, and they get money while they have killed people [laughs again].’’ Hakim 54 

Moreover, it is noteworthy that some irony can be noticed when talking about justice, which can also be seen in the above statement. The ironic undertone might have something to do with conflicting narratives. There seems to be a gap between the life narratives of the respondents and the master narratives of both the Afghan and the Dutch Governments. Master narratives refer to the narratives of legitimate authorities or institutions. What can be seen, is that the wish for justice has priority in the life narratives of the victims. However, the master narratives of both Governments do not include the desire for justice as its main priority. According to the respondents, the Afghan Government is still just as corrupt as it was during the Communist regime. Many of the offenders of the Communist regime, are now part of the current regime. In contrast, the Dutch Government does pay attention to this case, but according to the Afghan victims, not really enough. Despite the initiative of the Team International Crimes of the Dutch Government, ‘’There is not enough money and staff available to conduct a large-scale research.’’ Ghulam. Hence, the discrepancy between the life narratives of the victims and the master narratives of both governments might cause the painful undertone of irony. In turn, this gap might strengthen the victims’ sense of injustice. With an eye on the definition of Shklar (1990), it can be argued that the actions of both the Afghan Government and the Dutch Government do not meet the expectations of the Afghan victims. The victims seem to expect certain actions of both Governments, but were disappointed. As a result, these unfulfilled expectations contribute to their sense of injustice. 

Nevertheless, their experienced sense of injustice often leads to action. All respondents possess resentment with regards to the suffering inflicted on them and the impunity of their offenders. Here the redemption sequence comes into play. In order to contribute to justice in the future, many respondents are closely involved in human rights organisations or victims’ rights foundations, of which the AVR Foundation is a good example. Putting it like this, the victims’ involvement in organisations is often driven by their sense of injustice. 

Disbelief in justice 

The experience of so many different kinds of injustice seems to have caused a disbelief in justice. This disbelief already started during the regime. An important element of the regime was the so called ‘Special Revolutionary Court’, which imposed the prisoners a sentence. This court was part of the Communist Government and was considered an ideological court with only party members employed. After investigation and a certain period of time in the central prison, the prisoners were sent to this court to receive their verdict. 55 

‘’One day, they sent me to court. Well, it was not even a real court. There was a so called judge, and a so called public prosecutor who accused you of all sorts of nonsense.’’ Taleeb 

All respondents felt like the ‘Special Revolutionary Court’ did not offer a fair procedure. In addition to that, the misconducts the respondents were accused of were false, which furthered their disbelief in justice. 

‘’It was actually their own self-called court. We had absolutely no rights. We were not allowed to have a lawyer, we were not allowed to object, no altercation. ’’ Sabir 

The corruption continued after they got released. When the Communist Regime fell down, it was followed by the Mujahedeen and the Taliban which are both just as corrupt as the Communist regime. 

‘’After the Communist regime the Mujahedeen came. […] Again I had no job, knowledge was not that important anymore. Everything needed to be done according to the Islam. Everything changed again and there was no certainty in life. If you were on the side of the Government, you received privileges. Otherwise you would not survive.’’ Taleeb 

The rise of such powers strengthened the disbelief in legitimate authorities and their sense of injustice. The disbelief in justice of the Afghan victims continued in the Netherlands. As the above statements of Hakim and Ghulam show, they seem to have little trust in the Dutch authorities for two reasons. On the one hand it is argued that the Government provides money to (suspected) war crime offenders. On the other hand it is argued that Dutch authorities have not done enough so far; they should put more effort in the case of Afghanistan. This disbelief in justice might have an effect on their sense of communion. The Afghan victims once felt a sense of belongingness with the country Afghanistan. However, this country and its authorities turned out to be corrupt in all possible ways, which called into question their desire to feel connected to this country. In turn, their little trust in Dutch authorities possibly impedes the process of establishing a new sense of communion with the Dutch society. As in the case of Afghanistan, the diminished trust in the Dutch State calls into question the desire of belongingness with the Dutch society as well. 

Zooming out 

In addition to the discussion of the themes and the content of the life narratives, a broader picture of the life narratives will be sketched. This will be done by means of discussing the plotlines that appeared to be important in the Afghan victims’ narratives. Identifying these 56 

plotlines is important because people make sense of their world by framing their story into a plot. 

Plotlines 

Before diving into the specific plotlines of the victims’ life narratives, it needs to be stressed that all gathered life narratives differ in many respects from each other. However, all these different life narratives and plotlines seem to come together in two general plotlines. The first plotline that can be identified within the life narratives is called ‘What does not kill you…’, in which the fight for justice prevails despite the suffering. The second plotline that can be identified is ‘Tragedy’, in which the suffering prevails. Even though these plotlines are not a one-to-one fit, each life narrative of current research can be attributed to one of these plotlines. 

What does not kill you… 

With an eye on the life narratives of the Afghan victims and the plotline they choose, a combination of the ‘Quest’ plotline and the ‘Overcoming the Monster’ plotline appeared. To refresh the memory, the quest plotline is about the achievement of an ultimate goal and any effort will be made in order to accomplish this goal, often helped by companions. With an eye on the second theme, ‘the Greater Good’, and the way the respondents framed their own actions within their life narratives, the quest plotline can be identified. In light of current research and the life narratives, the priceless goal for the respondents was achieving freedom and independency for Afghanistan and its people. 

‘’I was against the occupation. I did not want to see people get killed for no reason. I wanted freedom, freedom to express my opinion. That was all.’’ Kabir 

Back in Afghanistan, they strived for this goal by means of participating in (student) resistance movements with companions, even though they knew the chances of getting caught. The respondents were willing to sacrifice their own freedom because they ultimately wanted to achieve freedom for Afghanistan and its citizens, as can be seen in the statement below. 

‘’’It is a dark and dangerous experience, but for me… It is very nice because they captured me for freedom, social justice. I am proud´´ Aamir 

Up to today, they fight for this ultimate goal, whether or not at a distance, as extensively described in the themes ‘Not Letting Go of Afghanistan’ and ‘Wish for Justice’. By means of their active participation in human rights organisations and victims’ rights organisations they try to contribute to the freedom and independency of Afghanistan. 57 

In short, the overcoming the monster plotline is about confronting a powerful monster in a fight to death. In the end, the hero wins the fight and gets a reward. In case of the life narratives of the Afghan victims, the regime can be considered the monster, possessing the freedom of the country, which is the treasure the respondents wanted to have. In the end, the regime fell down and the Afghan victims were released; this felt like a victory for them. 

‘’When I was at the Special Revolutionary Court, I received my verdict and I was taken away by officers. I laughed. Then the officers asked me: ‘’Why are you laughing?’’ and I answered: It is funny that you want to keep me in prison for 19 years. Do you really think your regime still exists in 19 years? I do not think so.’’ Taleeb 

During the interviews it became clear that it makes the respondents proud that they literally overcame the regime, i.e. the monster, and that they turned out to be stronger than the regime. What needs to be added to both plotlines, and the reason why they together make a new plotline, is the way the victims gave meaning to their victimhood after the experience of victimisation. In line with the redemption sequence, the victims made sense of their victimhood in a strengthened and impressive way. Their inhuman suffering did not kill them, but made them strong enough to fight against the wrongdoings they have faced. Many Afghan victims are still actively involved in several organisations in order to strive for justice and to be meaningful to the country Afghanistan. The identification of the redemption sequence within the life narratives is important because victims who make use of the redemption sequence often experience a better recovery from the traumatic event. In the long term, this will only strengthen their fight for justice and freedom of Afghanistan. Moreover, as elaborated in the themes ‘the Greater Good’ and ‘Wish for Justice’, doing something valuable for the country and its people contributes to their sense of agency and communion, which will only make them stronger after all. Important to note is that this plotline does not imply that these victims do not suffer at all. 

Tragedy 

The second plotline that can be distinguished from the life narratives is the tragedy plotline. To summarise, stories with a tragedy plotline have a tragic and sad theme and no happy ending. 

‘’My past is the core of my life, it is always in my mind. If I see things, hear certain stories, or talk about my experiences… I experience so many emotions and all the bad memories return. […] It is so exhausting and tiring for me.’’ Wahid 

The tragedy already became clear in the first theme, ‘Hidden Victimhood’. The past still chases the Afghan victims and it seems like their victimhood will never end. One of the tragic elements 58 

of the life narratives concerns the fact that the Afghan victims do not feel recognition and/or acknowledgement towards their victimhood. As a consequence, they never shared their stories with the Dutch society before, which impedes processing their trauma in the long term. # Chapter 6: Conclusion 

The narrative identity 

As explained in the third chapter, telling the life story is important because it contributes to the development of the narrative identity. To repeat briefly, the narrative identity structures the autobiographical past and future perspectives in such a way that it provides a certain degree of unity, purpose and meaning within the self. The narrative identity makes people capable of telling others who they are, how they came to be this way and how they see themselves in the future. Given the fact that people construct and internalise important aspects of the life story into an integrative story for life, i.e. the narrative identity, the narrative identity can be seen as the overarching concept. Therefore, in this final chapter all results come together: what do the life narratives of the Afghan victims ultimately say about their narrative identity? In the first place, it became clear from the interviews that the Afghan victims were not used to talk about their experiences of victimisation, especially not to an outsider. This might have impeded the establishment of their narrative identity; they lack the recurring interactions with other people, which are necessary for the development of the narrative identity. Furthermore, it is noticed during the interviews that the Afghan victims were able to provide detailed information about their victimhood. In contrast, they had less detailed information about their lives before the victimisation experience and after the victimisation experience. This is in line with the expectation as formulated in the theoretical framework; the life narratives of the Afghan victims are characterised by nuclear episodes. These nuclear episodes are of major importance within life narratives and serve as a script for present and future behaviour. This is also the case for the Afghan victims of this research. The Afghan victims’ nuclear episodes seem to have influenced the course of their life stories, hence the narrative identity, in two different ways. These two different ways can be traced to the two earlier explained plotlines: ‘What does not kill you…’ and ‘Tragedy’. What can be seen in both plotlines is that the perception of the self before the victimisation and after the victimisation has changed and caused a narrative rupture. However, the reaction to this narrative rupture differs per plotline and this results in a different development of the narrative identity. In case of the Afghan victims who can be attributed to the ‘What does not kill you…’ plotline, the nuclear episode evoked incredible combativeness among the victims. This sense of combativeness did not seem to be part of the self before the experience of victimisation. The experience of victimisation caused a narrative rupture and called into question their basic assumptions about their identity, meaning and life itself. The victimisation experiences during 61 

the regime gave the Afghan people a new identity: the identity of a victim. Their notions of, for example justice, are also affected immensely, as described in the themes ‘Wish for Justice’ and ‘Not Letting Go of Afghanistan’. However, this narrative rupture does not seem to have destroyed the narrative identity of the ‘What does not kill you…’ victims. They gave, in line with the redemption sequence, meaning to their victimhood and this in turn evoked their combativeness. This combativeness resulted in their fight against injustice and their involvement in human rights organisations and victims’ rights organisations, which they want to continue in the future. Through their sense- and meaning making processes, the victims transformed their nuclear episodes in redemptive present and future behaviour. It feels like they have restored their self-continuity in one way or another. In contrast, the victims’ life narratives of the ‘Tragedy’ plotline follow a different path. Here, the nuclear episode of the victimisation experience is followed by episodes of enduring suffering. The experience of victimisation turned the victims’ world upside down; all the beliefs and assumptions they once had, were doubted. As explained in the theme ‘Hidden Victimhood’, the experience of victimisation caused shattered assumptions about their world as a safe and virtuous place. To this day, the victims are not able to restore these shattered assumptions. As a consequence, they seem to face difficulties in maintaining their sense of self-continuity. This idea is reinforced by the fact that the victims of the tragedy plotline were often not able to formulate a future perspective or a future in relation to the self. They were not capable of connecting the past, the victimisation experience and the present into an integrative story for life that guides their future life story. As Aamir pointed out: ‘’Victims have no future.’’ As a result, the victims of the tragedy plotline face difficulties with the establishment of their narrative identity. A factor that impedes the development of the narrative identity for all Afghan victims, is the role of culture in their lives. Culture is an important aspect of the narrative identity; it provides narrative scripts which can be used to frame the life story. At the same time, culture is the aspect by which people incorporate their own experiences within the wider social environment. The Afghan victims of current research seem to experience a clash between cultures and corresponding narratives. On the one hand, they felt a sense of belongingness and communion with the country Afghanistan, the community they lived in, its people and the culture with all its norms and values. However, this sense of communion is disrupted because the master narrative of the Afghan Government turned out to be corrupt and to be the cause of their victimhood. On the other hand, they now live in the Netherlands where the master narrative of the Dutch Government is largely trusted by the Afghan victims. By largely it is 62 

meant that the Afghan victims feel safe within the country, but would prefer some more investigation into their situation (as described in the theme ‘Wish for Justice’). Moreover, their Afghan roots and cultural norms and values have no similarities with the Dutch culture and its norms and values. Therefore, the Afghan victims find it difficult to fit themselves in the Dutch culture. These conflicting cultures and narratives cause a clash. As a consequence, culture provides no stable framework for the Afghan victims and this impedes the development of their narrative identity. 

Reflection on the researcher 

Examining the narratives of the Afghan victims on the first period was a challenging task. I am amazed by the openness of the Afghan victims to talk to me about their most painful memories. Due to the fact that I never heard such terrible stories in real life before, the first interviews made a major impression on me. I was having a hard time being a professional and objective researcher and there were moments I was carried away by emotions, especially afterwards. Once the data collection progressed, I was more and more able to put their stories into perspective. I started to get used to my role as a researcher and I was less disconcerted after the interviews. At the same time, I noticed that my attention towards Afghanistan, their victimhood and personal stories touched them on a personal level. All respondents emphasized how meaningful it was for them to share their story. They felt grateful for the fact that someone made an effort to conduct scientific research. Some respondents even got emotional and this made clear how grievous the subject still is. As a result of this mutual trust between researcher and respondent, the stories that were told during the interviews were open and honest. Above all, listening to the life stories of the Afghan victims and subsequently analysing them was a valuable learning experience. 

Methodological reflection 

With an eye on the methodology, this research has several strengths. The narrative perspective and corresponding method were extremely relevant for the current topic. It contributes to a new and deeper understanding of the life narratives of the Afghan victims. Moreover, the sample size of this research is an advantage. The sample of 12 life narratives provides very rich and comprehensive data which greatly benefits the data analysis and the results. However, there are some marginal notes. An important disadvantage of current research is the presence of a translator during four of the interviews. Although the translators really did try their best to translate everything the respondent said, the researcher herself had no clue what 63 

was said. As a consequence, the researcher might have missed – accidentally – important information or the specific way in which the respondent framed and told their story. Another disadvantage of a translator is that it is unsure whether the respondent would have said the same things during the interview without the translator present. Underlying relationships between the respondent and the translator possibly influenced the content of the interview. Another marginal note concerns the bias of the sample. As shortly pointed out in the methodology chapter, the AVR Foundation served as a gatekeeper during the selection of the respondents and gathered respondents by means of the snowball sampling. As a consequence, the researcher had no control over the composition of the sample. Hence it is unclear whether the sample of current research is a representative reflection of the Afghan victims’ population residing in the Netherlands. 

Implications 

As far as known, this research is the first research to the victimhood of Afghan victims on the first period (1978-1992) residing in the Netherlands. Therefore this research should be considered the very first step. Further scientific research is needed in order to gain deeper insights into the life narratives of the Afghan victims and, ultimately, to win the combat against impunity. Current research can have several implications for future research. Current research only includes male victims and therefore only their life narratives are examined. This can be explained by the fact that the researcher herself had no access to the respondents and was dependent on the available respondents, which were all men. It might be interesting for future research to examine the narratives of female Afghan victims as well. # Abstract 

Background: On 27 April 1978, the Democratic Party of Afghanistan and the former Soviet Union committed a coup d’état. This coup was the starting point of an oppressive Communist regime in Afghanistan. Opponents of the regime were prosecuted, punished and murdered. Thousands of people fled to other countries and, inter alia, the Netherlands received 36.000 applications for asylum. Consequently, there is currently a fairly large victimised Afghan population in the Netherlands. However, there has never been attention to this specific group of victims before. Therefore this study examines the life narratives of Afghan victims residing in the Netherlands on the first period (1978-1992). 

Methodology: This research is conducted from a narrative perspective. The total data collection consists of 12 narrative interviews with Afghan victims residing in the Netherlands. All respondents are ex-political prisoners between the 48 and 71 years old. 

Results: The ‘zooming in’ on the narratives shows four main themes within the life narratives of Afghan victims residing in the Netherlands: ‘Hidden Victimhood’, ‘The Greater Good’, ‘Not Letting Go of Afghanistan’ and ‘Wish for Justice’. The ‘zooming out’ demonstrates how all different life narratives come together in two overarching, general plotlines: ‘What does not kill you…’ and ‘Tragedy’. Each life narrative of current research can be attributed to one of these plotlines. 

Conclusion: The life narratives of the Afghan victims residing in the Netherlands ultimately define the narrative identity in two different ways, coincide with the plotlines. Afghan victims from the ‘What does not kill you…’ plotline gave a valuable meaning to their victimhood and transformed their victimisation into redemptive behaviour. Despite the suffering, the victims seemed to be able to develop a narrative identity in one way or another. In contrast, the life narratives of the Afghan victims of the ‘Tragedy’ plotline are marked by enduring suffering. The victimisation experience destroyed all their beliefs in the world as a safe and virtuous place. Their sense of self-continuity is affected and therefore the victims face difficulties in formulating a future perspective. As a result, these victims have problems with the establishment of their narrative identity. 

Key words: Afghanistan, victimhood, life narratives, agency and communion, redemption, plotlines, the narrative identity 4
