Whitney Barnes went down for the count of one but bobbed up serenely.

Whitney Barnes saw the trembling lip and the dampening eye and strove to avert a catastrophe that would probably double the difficulty of probing into the mystery. Turning to Gladwin, but half directing his remarks to Helen, he said:

“I’ve just been telling the ladies that you and Travers are bosom pals.”

Travers Gladwin flashed one look of amazement and then caught on.

“Has he?” gasped Helen, looking into the young man’s brown eyes for confirmation, feeling that she liked the eyes, but uncertain that she read the confirmation.

“Yes, everything,” lied Gladwin, now glowing with enthusiasm.

All this while the shy and silent Sadie had remained demurely in her chair looking from one to the other and vainly endeavoring to catch the drift of the conversation.

Sadie was too dainty a little soul to be possessed of real reasoning faculties. The one thought that had been uppermost in her mind all day was that Helen was taking a desperate step, probably embarking upon some terrible tragedy. ## CHAPTER XV.

### HEROISM, LOVE AND SOMETHING ELSE.

The embarrassment of both the girls had begun to wear off. The two strange young men, notwithstanding the unaccounted-for absence of the object of Helen’s quest, began to appear less strange. Both possessed potent attractions and undeniable magnetism.

The shy and shrinking Sadie was sure she liked that tall and slender young man with the easy drawl and bright, humorous eyes immensely. The boldness of his glances made her heart beat pleasantly. Travers Gladwin’s psychic waves that had so utterly failed in the grill room of the Ritz may or may not have had something to do with this. ## CHAPTER XVI.

### THE TORMENT OF OFFICER 666.

Meantime Officer 666, on his aristocratic beat, four blocks up and four blocks down the Fifth avenue pave, was sticking to the east side of the street and vainly trying to keep his eyes to the front.

It was excruciating duty, with the raven-haired Rose wheeling her perambulator along the opposite way and keeping, by way of feminine perversity, on a latitudinal line with the patrolling of Michael Phelan.

There she was just opposite, always, never twisting her head an inch to give him so much as a glance or a smile. It made him wild that she should discipline her eyes in that fashion, while his would wander hither and yon, especially yon when Rose was in that direction.

The daintiness of Rose in cap and apron with a big white fichu at her throat, with one red cheek and the corner of the most kissable mouth on the avenue maddeningly visible, soon drove all memory of the Gladwin mansion and the suspicious antics of the “rat-faced little heathen” out of his mind. His one thought was that Rose would have to cross over the 97 way at the fall of dusk and trundle her millionaire infant charge home for its prophylactic pap. There would be a bare chance for about seven or ten words with Rose. But what was he going to say?

For one hundred and nine days’ running, his days off inclusive, Michael Phelan had intercepted Rose at that particular corner and begged her to name the day. The best he ever got was a smile and a flash of two laughing eyes, followed by the sally:

“Show me $500 in the bank, Michael Phelan, and I’ll talk business.”

And why didn’t Michael Phelan save up $500 out of the more than $100 a month the city paid him for his services? Rose didn’t get a quarter of that, and she had already saved $300, besides which she sent a one-pound note home to Ireland every month.

The reason was this––Michael Phelan turned in his wages each month to his mother, and out of what she allowed him to spend he couldn’t have saved $500 in five hundred years, at least not to his way of thinking. The trouble was that Rose had more than an inkling of this, and it galled her to think that her gallant brass-buttoned cop should permit himself to be still harnessed to his mother’s apron strings.

Yes, down in the invisible depths of Rose’s heart she was very fond of the faithful and long-suffering Michael, but even so she couldn’t bring herself to marry a milksop who was likely to make her play second fiddle to his mother. And when Rose once made 98 up her mind, she was as grimly determined as she was pretty.

The sun had swung down behind the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the trees that bordered the Park wall had begun to trace their shadows on the marble fronts of the mansions across the way when Rose suddenly wheeled the gig containing Master Croesus and walked demurely toward Officer 666.

Michael Phelan blushed till he could feel his back hair singeing, but he stopped stock still and waited. Rose gave no sign until she was within half a dozen feet of him. Then she looked up pertly and exclaimed:

“Why, if it ain’t Michael Phelan!”

“It is, Rose, an’ with the same question pantin’ on his lips,” broke out the young man, his bosom surging and his heart rapping under his shield.

“And what is that same question, Mr. Phelan?” asked the tantalizing Rose.

Abstract

Background: On 27 April 1978, the Democratic Party of Afghanistan and the former Soviet
Union committed a coup d’état. This coup was the starting point of an oppressive Communist
regime  in  Afghanistan.  Opponents  of  the  regime  were  prosecuted,  punished  and  murdered.
Thousands of people fled to other countries and, inter alia, the Netherlands received 36.000
applications  for  asylum.  Consequently,  there  is  currently  a  fairly  large  victimised  Afghan
population in the Netherlands. However, there has never been attention to this specific group
of victims before. Therefore this study examines the life narratives of Afghan victims residing
in the Netherlands on the first period (1978-1992).
Methodology:  This  research  is  conducted  from  a  narrative  perspective.  The  total  data
collection consists of 12 narrative interviews with Afghan victims residing in the Netherlands.
All respondents are ex-political prisoners between the 48 and 71 years old.
Results: The ‘zooming in’ on the narratives shows four main themes within the life narratives
of  Afghan  victims  residing  in  the  Netherlands:  ‘Hidden  Victimhood’,  ‘The  Greater  Good’,
‘Not Letting Go of Afghanistan’ and ‘Wish for Justice’. The ‘zooming out’ demonstrates how
all different life narratives come together in two overarching, general plotlines: ‘What does
not kill you…’ and ‘Tragedy’. Each life narrative of current research can be attributed to one
of  these  plotlines.
Conclusion: The life narratives of the Afghan victims residing in the Netherlands ultimately
define the narrative identity in two different ways, coincide with the plotlines. Afghan victims
from the ‘What does not kill you…’ plotline gave a valuable meaning to their victimhood and
transformed their victimisation into redemptive behaviour. Despite the suffering, the victims
seemed to be able to develop a narrative identity in one way or another. In contrast, the life
narratives of the Afghan victims of the ‘Tragedy’ plotline are marked by enduring suffering.
The  victimisation  experience  destroyed  all  their  beliefs  in  the  world  as  a  safe  and  virtuous
place. Their sense of self-continuity is affected and therefore the victims face difficulties in
formulating  a  future  perspective.  As  a  result,  these  victims  have  problems  with  the
establishment of their narrative identity.

Key words:  Afghanistan, victimhood, life narratives, agency and communion, redemption,
plotlines, the narrative identity

Chapter 1: Introduction
Tumultuous Afghanistan
As  long  as  can  be  remembered,  Afghanistan  is  tormented  by  ongoing  wars  and  conflicts.
Afghanistan,  officially  the  Islamic  Republic  of  Afghanistan,  is  a  country  in  Central  Asia
which  currently  has  around  31  million  residents.  As  a  consequence  of  all  the  turmoil  the
country  has  faced, Afghanistan nowadays is one of the most impoverished countries of the
world. It is a diverse and multi-ethnic country which is remarked by several micro-societies
with  flexible  boundaries.  The  largest  ethnic  group  consists  of  Pashtuns  (42  percent  of  the
population),  followed  by  Tajiks  (27  percent  of  the  population),  Hazaras  (9  percent  of  the
population), Uzbek (9 percent of the population) and Aimak (4 percent of the population) (UK
Border  Agency,  2013).  Afghanistan  is  predominantly  a  Muslim  country,  but  it  does  have
Hindu,  Sikh  and  Jewish  minorities  as  well  (Maley,  2009).  Even  today,  Afghanistan  faces
difficulties  that  to  a  great  extent  are  the  result  of  its  turbulent  history  and  its  difficult
geographical location (ICRC, 2010).  One of the major events Afghanistan has suffered
from  is  the  coup  d’état  committed  on  27  April  in  1978  by  the  Democratic  Party  of
Afghanistan (the PDPA) and the former Soviet Union (Halliday & Tanin, 1998). This coup
d’état was the starting point of the oppressive Communist regime in Afghanistan. Opponents
of the regime were harshly prosecuted, punished and murdered. This Communist oppression
lasted until 1992 when the regime fell down. As a result, thousands of citizens fled to Iran,
Pakistan, other neighbouring countries and Western (European) countries in the ‘90s (Hessels
&  Wassie,  2004).  Germany  appeared  to  be  the  most  popular  European  country  for  Afghan
refugees. Approximately 58.000 refugees applied for asylum between 1992 and 2002. After
Germany, the Netherlands was the most favoured European country. Between 1992 and 2002,
around 36.000 Afghan refugees applied for asylum and came to the Netherlands (Hessels &
Wassie,  2004).  These  numbers  are  relatively  high  compared  to  other  European  countries.
Great  Britain  for  example  received  29.000  applications  for  asylum,  while  Austria  received
around  26.000  requests,  France  less  than  2000  and  countries  such  as  Spain,  Finland  and
Ireland barely received applications for asylum (Hessels & Wassie, 2004).

Article 1F
In 1956, the Netherlands signed the Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, also known
as the UN Refugee Convention (Amnesty International, n.d.). With this Convention the Dutch
Government declared that protection will only be offered to those who have fled their home
country  for  fear  of  persecution  (IND,  n.d.).  However,  with  such  an  influx  of  refugees,  the

[PDF page 9]
chances were that suspects of war crimes or crimes against humanity would seek refuge in the
Netherlands, too.
This was also the case with the residing of immigrants in the Netherlands during the
‘90s from inter alia Afghanistan. To avoid being a place that harbours offenders, the Dutch
Government  formulated  article  1F.  Article  1F  discusses  war  crimes,  crimes  against  peace,
crimes against humanity and other serious crimes such as murder, rape and drugs trafficking
(IND,  n.d.).  In  case  of  serious  signs  of  commitment  of  one  of  these  crimes,  the  Dutch
Immigration  and  Naturalisation  service  (IND)  is  obliged  to  investigate  these  signals.  This
investigation  is  necessary  in  order  to  guarantee  real  victims  the  granted  protection  and  to
exclude possible offenders or suspects from this protection. When the IND suspects someone
responsible  for  war  crimes  or  crimes  against  humanity,  (s)he  gets  the  1F  status:  the
application for asylum will be rejected and (s)he is obliged to leave the country (IND, n.d.).

Afghans residing in the Netherlands
Due to the hazardous situation in Afghanistan and the flow of refugees as its consequence,
there is currently a fairly large Afghan population residing in the Netherlands. However, the
issue that arises is that very little is known about this population; it is unclear exactly how
many serious offenders of war crimes are among them. In 2012, the estimation was made that
around 190 Afghan people with 1F status were residing in the Netherlands (Tweede Kamer,
2012). These so called ‘1F people’ did not get asylum but the chances are that they are still
illegally living in the Netherlands (Pietersen, 2012). The 1F people barely receive (political)
attention but if there is attention, it is mainly focused on the offenders.
The  victims  from  Afghanistan  are  often  forgotten.  They  experienced  traumatising
events  in  Afghanistan  and  fled  to  the  Netherlands  in  order  to  escape  from  the  dangerous
situation.  Yet  they  live  in  the  same  country  as  their  offenders.  The  one  who,  for  example,
tortured or killed family members of the victims back in Afghanistan, now enjoys the same
rights  within  the  same  country  and  does  not  suffer  from  the  past.  Sometimes  victim  and
offender  even  live  in  the  same  neighbourhood.  This  can  be  very  confrontational.  For  the
victims it is very painful that their side of the story has been neglected so far. Their stories are
never heard while the experience of victimisation is still an important part of their lives.

The Afghan Victims’ Rights Foundation
Despite  the  lack  of  public  attention  towards  the  Afghan  victims,  there  are  some  victim
initiatives. An example of an organisation that represents the interests of these Afghan victims
is the Afghan Victims’ Rights Foundation (AVR). The AVR Foundation has several aims, but

[PDF page 10]
their  main  goal  is  to  combat  the  impunity  of  all  the  war  suspects  (AVR,  n.d.).  Other  aims
relate  to  their  wish  to  give  the  victims  and  their  relatives  a  voice.  They  want  to  share  the
victims’ stories and make them known. Furthermore, in order to  accommodate the victims,
the organisation serves as a platform for contact, awareness, actions and collaboration among
the victims. They do so by means of organising meetings and memorial(s) where all victims
come together as fellow sufferers. Finally, the AVR Foundation wants to expand the limited
knowledge  concerning  the  Communist  regime  and  its  atrocities.  By  documenting  witness
statements,  evidence  and  literature  about  the  violations,  they  want  to  expand  the  existing
knowledge  and  inform  people  about  what  happened  in  Afghanistan.  Ultimately,  these
documented statements, evidence and literature can contribute to the combat against impunity.

Victims’ narratives
Every aspect of human life is characterised and surrounded by stories. Such stories are also
called narratives. There are numerous kinds of narratives: personal stories people tell to each
other, media items, stories in books, history, myths and so on. Every human being, and hence
each victim, has its own (life) story or narrative that includes important experiences, dates and
events.  These  life  narratives  are  important  because  the  reality  of  human  experience  can  be
seen as one which has a narrative or storytelling character. As Crossley (2000, p. 10) points
out: ‘’Lives are told in being lived and lived in being told.’’ Life narratives do not necessarily
imply  true  or  factual  accounts  of  what  happened,  rather  it  reflects  the  personal,  and  hence
subjective, experience of an individual of a certain event. The function of these narratives is
that  it  influences  future  behaviour  (Sandberg,  2010).  Furthermore,  when  people  talk  about
their experiences, they do not randomly choose language and meaning for their story. Rather
they lean on ways of self-presenting and thinking that they have used and learned somewhere
else or in the past (Sandberg, 2010). Ultimately, out of the life story, people need to construct
and  internalise  important  aspects  into  an  integrative  story  for  life,  this  is  also  called  the
narrative  identity  (McAdams  &  McLean,  2013).  The  narrative  identity  allows  people  to
express  who  they  are,  how  they  came  to  be  this  way  and  how  they  see  themselves  in  the
future.
However,  the  life  narrative  becomes  affected  when  an  individual  is  victimised.  The
experience of victimisation often concerns the most important episode within the life story.
Experiencing severe victimisation calls into question basic assumptions and beliefs about how
the  world  works;  it  affects  the  perception  of  safety,  justice  and  predictability  (Pemberton,
2015). Moreover, it threatens an individual’s taken-for-granted notions about time, identity,

[PDF page 11]
meaning  and  life  itself  (Crossley,  2000).  The  experience  of  victimisation  thus  affects  the
human’s existence. However, in one way or another, victims have to give meaning and sense
to their experience and they have to try to incorporate the experience of victimisation in their
life story. For victims this can be a very challenging task. They need to transform their life
story in which they connect the past, the victimisation, the present and the future into a new
whole (Pemberton, 2015). In other words, the experience of victimisation doubts the narrative
identity; it impedes their expression of who they are as a person, what shaped them and how
they perceive themselves in the future.

Current Research
The lack of (public) attention towards the Afghan victims residing in the Netherlands is very
painful for the AVR Foundation. Given the fact that research into to Afghan victims has never
been conducted before, the AVR Foundation asked for a scientific study to their victimhood.
With  this  in  mind,  current  research  intends  to  give  a  voice  to  a  group  of  victims  that  felt
neglected and has never been heard before. With the eye on the notion that the experience of
victimisation has an enormous impact on the victims’ life narratives and everything it entails,
this research is conducted from a narrative perspective. The use of the narrative perspective in
research into the concept of the victimhood is a new approach, and this makes current study
scientifically relevant.
To  understand  what  the  experience  of  victimisation  has  done  and  still  does  to  the
Afghan  victims’  narratives  and  their  narrative  identity,  it  is  important  to  focus  not  only  on
their victimisation, but on their whole life story by examining the past, the victimisation, the
present and the future. In order to gain insight in the life narratives of the Afghan victims, this
thesis examines the following research question: What are the narratives of Afghan victims
residing in the Netherlands on the first period (1978-1992)?
To answer this question, this thesis will start with a historical overview of the events
that  have  happened  in  Afghanistan  during  the  Communist  regime  (1978-1992).  Then  there
will  be  a  theoretical  framework  concerning  the  importance  of  narratives  in  relation  to
victimisation. The third chapter will be about the research method of this thesis. This will be
followed  by  the  results  of  the  research  and  a  linkage  will  be  made  with  the  historical  and
theoretical notions. Finally, there will be a conclusion.

Chapter 2: The Afghan History
Lack of knowledge
Analysing  the  Afghan  Communist  Regime  and  all  its  events  is  still  relevant  today.  The
oppressive PDPA Regime has had much influence on the modern Afghan history and on the
way  Afghanistan  is  constructed  nowadays.  During  the  14-year  regime  the  country  was
transformed and changed, from above and below, and it dealt with Soviet forces that entered
the country. This ultimately led to the chaos of the 1990s in which a new radical, authoritarian
faction  came  to  power:  the  Taliban  (Halliday  &  Tanin,  1998).  With  the  eye  on  current
research,  it  is  important  to  understand  what  has  happened  in  Afghanistan  during  the
Communist regime and what the direct aftermath of this regime entailed. Only when this is
taken into account, it is possible to comprehend the visions and perspectives of the victims of
the regime, which is central in this thesis.
However,  constructing  the  Afghan  history  is  extremely  difficult  for  several  reasons.
The  ongoing  war  in  Afghanistan  has  annihilated  many  social-  and  political  institutions,  it
caused the death of more than one million people and more than six million people fled to
other  countries  as  a  refugee  or  a  permanent  exile  (War  Crimes  Research  Office,  2014).
Furthermore, most Afghan intellectuals were either killed or they fled during the Communist
Regime.  This  is  problematic  because  these  intellectuals  were  most  capable  of  documenting
the events. Another difficulty is related to the fact that the leadership of Afghanistan during
the  regime  has  changed  frequently  over  time  (War  Crimes  Research  Office,  2014).  This
resulted  in  a  limited  documentation  of  the  events  during  the  Communist  Regime  in
Afghanistan.
In the beginning of the conflict, no international human rights organisations and hardly
any  journalists  were  able  to  enter  the  country  (War  Crimes  Research  Office,  2014).
Institutions  like  the  United  Nations  (UN)  and  international  human  rights  groups  started  to
explore  the  events,  but  their  documentation  and  testimonies  are  very  much  limited  in  this
early period. From 1980, the documentation of the atrocities somewhat improved. The first
Afghan  refugees  settled  in  neighbouring  countries  and  started  to  tell  stories  about  the
conditions in Afghanistan. Additionally, journalists, human rights organisations and the UN
started to send delegations to refugee camps and sometimes even to Afghanistan itself (War
Crimes Research Office, 2014). Human rights reports from this period contain interviews with
the refugees and therefore they can serve as first-hand testimonies.
Nevertheless,  there  are  some  marginal  notes.  The  interviews  on  which  the  human
rights  reports  are  based  are  not  available;  only  the  reports  can  be  accessed.  Moreover,  the

[PDF page 13]
reports  only  include  stories  of  refugees  to  whom  the  investigators  had  access.  Almost  all
involved organisations only sent investigators to Pakistan and not to Iran, because Iran did not
allow rapporteurs until 2002. However, approximately half of the Afghan refugees fled to Iran
since  1978  and  thus  their  stories  are  largely  missing  (War  Crimes  Research  Office,  2014).
Finally, multiple human rights reports wrote about the committed atrocities of the PDPA, the
Soviet  forces  and  the  security  force  called  Khadamat-e  Aetla’at-e  Dawlati  (KhAD).  These
reports entail information about their arrests, torture, detention conditions, bombardments and
reprisals  against  the  inhabitants  of  Afghanistan  (War  Crimes  Research  Office,  2014).
However,  the  atrocities  committed  by  resistance  forces  in  Afghanistan  and  Pakistan  are
missing  in  these  reports.  These  acts  were  only  documented  from  1988  onwards  and  that  is
why the human rights reports cannot be regarded as complete.
In order to provide a solid historical framework, several different literature sources are
used. The used articles have been selected carefully and have various strengths. For example,
the  articles  of  Halliday  and  Tanin  (1998)  and  the  UK  Border  Agency  (2013)  give  an
extensive, chronological and coherent overview of the history. Such overviews are scarce and
therefore these articles were exceptionally helpful. While the article of Halliday and Tanin is
somewhat biased (it only sheds light on the atrocities of the regime), the article of the War
Crimes Research Office (WCRO, 2014) compensates this flaw. The WCRO is a legal institute
that provides an objective report about the Afghan history, written from an outsider’s point of
view. Furthermore, both the articles of the UK Border Agency and author  Ishiyama (2005)
put the Afghan history in a broader (political) context and represent the history from multiple
perspectives. This approach is interesting because it provides a deeper understanding of the
country Afghanistan and it gives insight in the different views of one and the same history.
While constructing the Afghan history and its events, the weaknesses of the articles were kept
in mind and the strengths were utilised.
With an eye on the importance of narratives and the narrative perspective within this
research, it is interesting to see that literature sources like history books and articles can also
be considered narratives. Without a doubt, the Afghan history consists of facts and details of
true events during the Communist regime. These historical facts and details are included in
the Afghan historic accounts. However, the way this history is written, constructed and placed
in  a  certain  context,  might  say  something  about  the  writer  and  its  perspective  and/or
perception. In turn, the way an article or book is read and interpreted, possibly says something
about the perspective and/or perception of the reader. This interplay needs to be taken into
account  not  only  while  constructing  this  historical  framework,  but  also  while  reading  this

[PDF page 14]
historical framework.
As  might  be  clear,  the  available  literature  sources  about  the  Afghan  history  are
somewhat limited and therefore constructing the history of Afghanistan is not straightforward.
Despite  the  lack  of  literature,  an  attempt  is  made  to  give  a  clear  overview  of  the  history.
However, it is important to keep in mind that, just like the literature, this historical framework
might have some gaps.

Revolution from above
Before giving a historical overview of the events that have taken place in Afghanistan, some
general information about the regime should be provided first. The Afghanistan Communist
Regime can be considered a revolution from above, also referred to as the Saur revolution.
That means, the introduction and imposition of a set of changes by a radical faction within the
State  committed  to  a  forced  modernisation  of  the  country  (Halliday  &  Tanin,  1998).  With
regards to modernisation, the adherents of the Communist regime wanted to catch up as soon
as  possible  with  the  rest  of  the  world.  The  revolution  caused  a  clash  between  ideological
radicalisation at the top and the indigenous society below (Ishiyama, 2005). A major part of
the  radicals  were  intellectuals,  other  adherents  were  military  men  or  urban  professionals.
These radicals were seen as the product of an education system based in the capital. However,
the radicals were a relatively small group compared to the indigenous group of Afghans, also
called  conservative  or  rural  Afghans.  To  give  an  idea:  in  1978,  during  the  coup  d’état,  the
active members of the PDPA made up only one percent of the total society and only three to
five percent of the civilians supported the PDPA (Ishiyama, 2005).
Although the coup d’état of the PDPA regime was in 1978, the PDPA as a party was
established back in 1965 (Ishiyama, 2005). Soon thereafter, the PDPA party was split up into
two  different  factions:  Khalq  and  Parcham,  which  became  rivals  later  on.  The  PDPA  was
established  by  a  group  of  individuals,  these  intellectuals  strived  to  achieve  secular
modernisation in Afghanistan. This went hand in hand with the Afghan Government’s desire,
with  support  of  the  PDPA,  to  obtain  a  more  ‘loose  approach’  of  the  Islam.  However,  the
conservative and rural Afghans, the majority of the population, turned out not to be ready for
such a change and resisted (Maley, 2009). In order to achieve this loose approach of the Islam
anyway, the Afghan Government sought support from outside the country. Here, the Soviet
Union (the USSR, as mentioned above) came in. The Soviet Union was then involved in the
Cold  War  (1945-1989)  and  wanted  to  expand  their  Communist  imperium.  As  a  result,
Afghanistan was the scene of the last large-scale clash of the Cold War. The occupation by

[PDF page 15]
the Soviet Union between 1979 and 1989 caused an atrocious war, which will be elaborated
below (ICRC, 2010).

Part I: Before 1978
Before the Communist Regime came to power, Afghanistan had been a monarchy since the
eighteenth century (Kakar, 1978). But during the 1950s, there was a growing dissatisfaction
within the monarchy; modernists argued that the development of Afghanistan was too slow in
comparison to the rest of the world. In order to accelerate this development, three new men
stood  up  as  leaders  of  the  country:  Muhammad  Zahir,  Muhammad  Daud  and  Sardar
Muhammad. Especially Muhammad Daud became an important man; he became the head of
the Government for the next decade (Kakar, 1978). Muhammad Daud started to reform the
country;  he  built  up  the  army,  he  improved  the  infrastructure  and  he  made  socioeconomic
changes. These reforms were possible because of the support he had gained from the Soviet
Union (Kakar, 1978). As a result of the changes Muhammad Daud had made, an assertive and
proactive middle class was born. This middle class was no longer satisfied with the reign of
the  monarchy  and  they  wanted  to  embrace  more  Western  aspects  in  their  lifestyle.  This
encouraged  Daud  to  continue  his  reforms  and  to  make  it  more  political (Kakar,  1978).  His
interventions  seemed  to  threaten  the  rule  of  the  monarchy  and  therefore  he  was  forced  to
resign as prime minister in 1963 (UK Border Agency, 2013).
A constitutional period dawned and a group of intellectual liberals took place in the
Government,  while  the  king  was  still  a  central  figure.  During  this  period,  people  got  more
(political) freedom and they became more advanced than their neighbouring countries (Kakar,
1978).  The  Government  was  no  longer  considered  rigid;  on  the  contrary,  the  Government
seemed to be soft. However, this liberalisation of Afghanistan went hand in hand with new
problems. The embracement of the Western lifestyle brought Western-oriented crimes into the
cities,  such  as  burglary  and  robbery,  and  the  country  did  not  know  how  to  cope  with  such
crimes. To the dismay of the conservatives and religious adherents, this caused another type
of chaos within the society (Kakar, 1978). This dissatisfaction had its peak during the 1970s.
Tensions  arose  between  all  the  different  groups:  the  monarchy,  intellectuals,  modernists,
conservatives and religious leaders. These tensions ultimately led to the end of the monarchy.
On  July  17  in  1973,  Muhammad  Daud,  the  former  prime  minister,  overthrew  the
monarchy in a coup (UK Border Agency, 2013). He became the man in power and declared
Afghanistan  a  Republic.  Daud  was  capable  of  committing  such  a  coup  due  to  an  unstable
political  situation  with  barely  any  authority  for  the  Government  (Ridout,  1975).  In  the

[PDF page 16]
following  years,  Daud  continued  the  modernisation  of  the  country  and  he  focused  on  the
development  of  the  economy.  In  the  first  instance,  Daud  got  support  from  the  PDPA.
However, the PDPA started to withdraw once they noticed that Daud wanted to have all the
power  (Migratieweb,  2000).  Once  again,  tensions  emerged  within  Afghanistan,  this  time
between Daud and the PDPA.
Afghanistan was extremely weak and fragmented due to colonial power and the lack
of a unified state power prior to 1978 (Halliday & Tanin, 1998). As a result, the Afghan State
was limited to the major cities and dependent on foreign revenues (Halliday & Tanin, 1998).
Additionally,  there  was  no  effective  control  within  the  country  and  this  resulted  in  a  weak
state  without  infrastructural  and  absolute  power,  open  borders  and  a  dysfunctional
bureaucracy  with  massive  corruption  and  embezzlement  (Halliday  &  Tanin,  1998;  Maley,
2009).

Part II: Regime under the Democratic Party of Afghanistan (1978-1979)
The Amin period
As mentioned in the introduction chapter, the PDPA took over in April 1978 by means of a
coup  d´état,  also  known  as  the  Saur  revolution.  As  mentioned  earlier,  the  aim  of  this
revolution  was  to  accomplish  secular  modernisation.  To  achieve  this  goal,  the  PDPA
overthrew the Government of Muhammad Daud, who ruled since his own coup in 1973. The
Saur revolution was possible with the help of the Soviet Union (USSR), but within the society
there was barely any commitment to Soviet Communism (Halliday & Tanin, 1998). From the
start, the leadership of the PDPA regime was in hands of the Khalq faction. Two important
men within the Kalq faction were Nur Muhammad Taraki and Hafiullah Amin. The latter was
at first a foreign minister of the PDPA and he later became the leader of the regime (Ishiyama,
2005).  The  Khalq  leadership  was  extremely  dominant:  they  rejected  any  collaboration  or
coalition with existing political parties and simultaneously denied the existing parties the right
to perform political activities (Halliday & Tanin, 1998).
With  the  Khalq  faction  in  control,  horrible  acts  were  committed.  They  harshly  and
violently  repressed  multiple  groups  within  the  Afghan  society:  the  intelligentsia,  political
figures  from  earlier  regimes,  local  notables,  religious  leaders  and  members  of  the  Parcham
faction (Halliday & Tanin, 1998; Ishiyama, 2005). All these groups needed to be repressed in
order to protect the people and make a success of the Saur revolution. The Parcham faction
was the primary target of massive purges. Parcham members and adherents were sent abroad
to execute diplomatic functions. However, after a while it became clear that the majority of

[PDF page 17]
these members were violently arrested and/or executed (Halliday & Tanin, 1998).

From  the  beginning  of  the  regime,  the  PDPA  used  torture  to  punish  suspected
opponents of the regime and at the same time they used it as a tool during interrogation (War
Crimes Research Office, 2014). The PDPA regime treated suspected detainees in a horrific
way.  The  circumstances  within  prison  were  extremely  poor  and  especially  detainees  in  the
largest prison of Afghanistan, Pul-e-Charkhi, suffered. On  a daily basis, the detainees were
humiliated, tortured and threatened with death. This is confirmed by a special report of the
United  Nations  (War  Crimes  Research  Office,  2014).  Detainees  talked  to  a  UN  Special
Rapporteur  and  they  declared  that  the  treatment  of  suspected  detainees  consisted  of:  sleep
deprivation, tearing out of fingernails, burns of various types, electric charges and sometimes
the use of electrical generators (War Crimes Research Office, 2014).
Additionally, an important goal of the Khalq oppression was the purge  of the army,
police  and  security.  All  generals  and  high-ranking  officers  of  the  previous  regime(s)  were
arrested or dismissed. At the same time, the Communist Regime dismissed officers who were
suspected  of  sympathy  for  the  Islamic  oppression.  Even  though  the  oppression  induced  a
widespread, rebellious resistance and large-scale emigration, it continued (Halliday & Tanin,
1998). The support for other non-Khalq officers increased and a resistance movement arose.
However,  Amin  kept  arresting  possible  threats  in  order  to  keep  his  own  position  safe.
Nevertheless, despite internal and external threats, Amin’s regime did not collapse until 1979.

Part III: Regime under Soviet occupation (1980-1992)
The Karmal period
The  Amin  Regime  came  to  an  end  when  Soviet  troops  invaded  in  December  1979.
Afghanistan,  especially  its  economy,  was  still  dependent  on  support  of  the  Soviet  Union
(Ishiyama, 2005). The disadvantage of this dependency was that it was practically impossible
for the PDPA to establish an independent, revolutionary movement. The support of the USSR
was needed in order to sustain the Afghan state, but at the same time caused this dependency
of the USSR a confined ability to gain normative support (ICRC, 2010).
At the behest of the Soviets, Amin was killed and the leadership came in hands of the
Parcham faction, with Babrak Karmal as one of its leading members (Halliday & Tanin, 1998;
Ishiyama, 2005). Unlike the Amin Government, the new Government of Karmal was largely
controlled by the Soviet Union (War Crimes Research Office, 2014). People who supported
Amin during the oppression lost their positions and were arrested or killed. Remarkably, a lot

[PDF page 18]
of  Khalq  officers  agreed  with  the  new  leadership  and  remained  in  their  old  positions.
Karmal’s priority was to expand the PDPA regime and its membership. In an attempt to do
this, he strengthened both the civilian and the military apparatus.
The development of military and security forces is the greatest achievement of Karmal
during  the  ‘80s.  Border  troops  were  established,  as  well  as  obligatory  military  service
(Halliday  &  Tanin,  1998).  Other  important  military  forces  were  the  military  police  and
paramilitary  groups.  The  latter  includes  the  Khidamat  –  i  Ittila’at  –  i  Dawlati  (KhAD):  a
security  force  under  the  leadership  of  Dr.  Najibullah,  that  acted  as  a  powerful  independent
ministry. The KhAD was established in 1980 and became an essential institution in the overall
construction  of  the  PDPA  imperium:  it  was  the  most  effective  instrument  of  Kabral’s
oppression. The KhAD served as the core of political influence and economic privileges and it
served  as  the  main  instrument  for  controlling  cities  and  conducting  counter-guerrilla
operations  (Halliday  &  Tanin,  1998).  With  the  advent  of  the  KhAD,  torture  practices  had
become  permanent  in  Afghanistan  (War  Crimes  Research  Office,  2014).  Torture  by  the
KhAD  took  place  in  multiple  prisons  in  Afghanistan.  The  main  location  of  their  torture
practices was their headquarters at Sedarat, which consisted of a central interrogation office,
eight detention centres and approximately 200 individual houses used for torture (War Crimes
Research Office, 2014). All political detainees were forced to interrogation, which included
multiple  acts  of  torture:  they  were  beaten  with  several  kinds  of  instruments,  abused  in
multiple  ways,  sleep  deprivation,  forced  to  stand  for  an  infinite  period,  forced  to  stand  in
water  or  in  snow,  electric  shocks,  physical  abuses  like  having  a  bottle  into  the  rectum,
fingernails pulled out or needles inserted under them, cut with a knife, burned with cigarettes
or boiling water and having hair torn out (War Crimes Research Office, 2014).
During the mid-term of the regime (1985-1989), the regime became relatively stable.
There  was  still  Soviet  support  and  therefore  it  was  possible  to  keep  control.  Karmal  was
capable of regulating the major cities and to keep the lines of communication open (Halliday
&  Tanin,  1998).  However,  the  effects  of  the  oppressive  regime  were  dramatically  visible
within  the  society.  The  people  suffered;  two  to  five  million  civilians  fled  to  neighbouring
countries and another one to two million people shifted from the countryside to rural areas.
Despite the relative stability, there were increasing problems for Karmal. He had difficulties
with  establishing  authority  in  the  conquered  (rural)  areas,  because  only  a  few  people
supported  the  Regime  of  Karmal  in  these  areas.  In  an  attempt  to  solve  this  reoccurring
problem,  Babrak  Karmal  was  replaced  by  Najibullah  in  1986,  the  General  Secretary  of  the
PDPA and the leader of the earlier mentioned KhAD.

[PDF page 19]
Part IV: The last phase of the regime
The Najibullah period
The  new  leadership  from  Najibullah  meant  new  directions  for  the  Afghan  Society.  With
Najibullah as leader, the last period of the Communist Regime started (Ishiyama, 2005). Soon
after  the  replacement  of  Kabral,  the  KhAD  was  transformed  into  a  new,  distinct  ministry
called  Wazarat-e  Amaniat-e  Dowlati  (WAD).  However,  the  WAD  had  largely  the  same
function  as  the  KhAD  (Migratieweb,  2000).  The  abuse  and  torture  practices  continued,
although  not  at  the  same  level  (War  Crimes  Research  Office,  2014).  Even  though  the
leadership  of  the  regime  had  changed,  there  was  still  much  pressure  on  the  Communist
Regime. In an attempt to lessen this pressure, Najibullah tried to execute a policy of national
reconciliation (Migratieweb, 2000).  In  contrast  to  his  predecessors,  Najibullah  was  more
successful  in  establishing  certain  links  between  the  State  and  the  (indigenous)  society
(Ishiyama, 2005). He reconstructed the building of the institution and this was visible in three
separate  ways  (Halliday  &  Tanin,  1998).  First  of  all,  Najibullah  wanted  to  increase  the
diversification  within  the  military  forces  of  the  regime.  He  developed  new  military  units,
called Special Guard under the command of the WAD (or KhAD). At the same time he kept
the other military forces (including the Khalqis) satisfied. Secondly, Najibullah systematically
dismissed  significant  people  of  influence  within  the  PDPA.  This  was  necessary  in  order  to
offer  former  KhAD  personnel  promotion  into  high-ranking  positions  (Halliday  &  Tanin,
1998). Finally, under the guidance of Najibullah the PDPA tried to recruit tribesmen to the
PDPA by a more traditional policy of inducements, this included arms and money. As part of
this process, he developed, for example, the National Compromise Commission to contact the
opponents of the Regime (Ishiyama, 2005). His argumentation behind this idea was that the
PDPA should lessen its military face and character towards the Afghan population (Halliday
& Tanin, 1998).
In  the  meantime,  there  was  growing  attention  for  Islamic  fundamental  rules  in  the
reign and inhabitants were allowed to establish political parties. These reforms were pursued
by a new constitution in 1987; Afghanistan officially became a Republic with Dr. Najibullah
as its first president (Migratieweb, 2000). Despite these successful changes, the Soviet Union
and the WAD were still of extreme importance for the existence of the regime.
With  these  new  directions,  Najibullah  attempted  to  establish  a  new  system  in
Afghanistan.  However,  the  identification  with  tribal  and  militia  forces  led  to  a  greater

[PDF page 20]
exposure to political difficulties. An additional problem was the collapse of the Soviet Union
in 1991 (Ishiyama, 2005; Maley, 2009). The Soviet troops already started to withdraw in May
1988  under  the  Geneva  accords,  and  this  withdrawal  was  a  fact  in  February  1989
(Migratieweb, 2000). For a few years Najibullah seemed capable of sustaining the regime, but
when financial support and the provision of resources of the USSR stopped, it became clear
that  the  regime  would  soon  collapse  without  Soviet  support  (ICRC,  2010).  All  these
difficulties resulted in an inevitable fragmentation of the Regime in 1992.

Part V: The direct aftermath
In 1992, after 14  years of harsh regime, the Afghan society was completely destroyed. The
combination  of  the  extremely  high  mortality  rates,  the  atrocious  war  crimes  and  the  large-
scale human rights violations affected the society in all possible ways. The Afghan population
was uprooted, social, economic and political institutions were destroyed or at least damaged
and people no longer felt safe and at home in their once so familiar country Afghanistan. To
give  an  impression:  between  1978  and  1987,  every  day  approximately  240  Afghan  people
were  killed  (ICRC,  2010).  Moreover,  as  a  result  of  the  harsh  regime,  a  major  part  of  the
Afghan population was displaced and forced to migrate to other countries. Almost half of the
population had left the country and lived somewhere else as a refugee. This caused long-term
problems concerning social disruption which is observable even today (ICRC, 2010).
An additional problem arose in the refugee camps in Pakistan during the ‘90s. These
camps  did  not  offer  protection  to  the  innocent  refugees  of  Afghanistan,  it  also  seemed  to
stimulate  combatants.  The  refugee  camps  turned  out  to  be  a  breeding  ground  for  a  new
oppressive  regime  of  the  Mujahedeen  and  the  Taliban,  which  soon  came  to  power  in
Afghanistan (ICRC, 2010).
Nowadays,  Afghanistan  is  still  in  harsh  conflict  with  the  Taliban.  According  to  the
United Nations, the number of civilians killed or wounded, due to Afghanistan’s conflict with
the  Taliban,  reached  its  peak  in  the  first  half  year  of  2016  (Rahim  &  Jamieson,  2016).  As
might be clear, ever since the fall of the regime until today, Afghanistan has been subject to
many changes. The country is still afflicted by continuous wars and conflicts.

Part VI: The Netherlands nowadays
From  1996,  multiple  people  from  different  countries  residing  in  the  Netherlands  were
suspected of international crimes. Once the Dutch Government noticed this, they wanted to
combat this impunity and they wanted to investigate these cases (Openbaar Ministerie, n.d.).
The Dutch State set up a special research team (Team International Crimes) which performs,

[PDF page 21]
in  collaboration  with  the  national  prosecutor  and  the  criminal  investigation  department,
criminal investigations to international crimes by or against Dutch people or people who are
residing in the Netherlands (Openbaar Ministerie, n.d.).
Since 2008, Afghanistan is under special attention of the Team International Crimes.
Due to the relatives of the Afghan victims who reported to the Dutch police, the Government
decided to investigate the Afghan suspects residing in the Netherlands. As mentioned in the
introduction  chapter,  approximately  190  people  with  1F  status  are  currently  living  in  the
Netherlands.  However,  so  far  only  three  cases  appeared  in  court.  Of  these  three  cases,  one
suspect is acquitted because of a lack of proof (Openbaar Ministerie, 2015.). Until today, the
criminal investigations of Afghan suspects residing in the Netherlands continue, but the lack
of proof seems to be an ongoing and intractable problem. In order to pursue and accelerate
their  combat  against  impunity,  the  Dutch  State  encourages  witnesses  and  relatives  of  the
Afghan victims to report to the police or to deliver a witness statement (Openbaar Ministerie,
2015).

Chapter 3: Narratives of Afghan Victims
As  can  be  read  in  the  historical  framework,  a  lot  has  happened  in  Afghanistan  during  the
Communist regime and an attempt is made to present an objective overview of the history.
However, behind this bigger story, there are numerous personal stories of people who have
experienced  the  Communist  regime  and  the  aftermath  themselves.  Many  of  them  suffered
during the regime and experienced severe forms of victimisation. However, research to the
victimhood of these Afghan victims has never been conducted before.
The  experience  of  victimisation  has  a  narrative  quality  (Pemberton,  2015)  and  the
victimisation is often of great importance in someone’s life story. In order to gain insight in
the  narratives  of  the  Afghan  victims  and  to  be  able  to  analyse  the  way  the  experience  of
victimisation  has  shaped  their  stories,  this  research  is  done  from  a  narrative  perspective.
Before  diving  into  the  narratives  of  the  Afghan  victims,  it  is  necessary  to  first  explain
(general) theoretical notions concerning the narrative perspective. Then it will be elaborated
how these narratives can be analysed and which techniques will be used. Subsequently, it will
be discussed what needs to be taken into account when zooming in on the narratives of the
Afghan victims; which themes are important within life stories, and in particular within life
stories  of  (Afghan)  victims,  and  why?  Finally,  attention  will  be  paid  to  the  plotlines  of
narratives: what plotline stands out when zooming out on the narratives? It will be explained
why  it  is  important  to  identify  plotlines  within  life  stories,  which  plotlines  exist,  and  how
these plotlines can be linked to the experience of victimisation.

The narrative perspective
The life story
Every human being is a natural storyteller. Human beings construct stories about their own
life and its particular experiences and they give meaning to them in a certain way (McAdams
& McLean, 2013). These kinds of stories are called life stories. Each life story differs in its
coherence, structural complexity and comprehensibility. Within this research, the concept of
the life story is interpreted and used in the following way: a subjective story about the events
in  life  as  told,  remembered  and  thought  by  an  individual  (Habermas  &  Bluck,  2000).
A  life  story  can  be  seen  as  an  internalised  narrative  of  the  life,  which  includes  the
reconstructed past, the perceived present and the future (McAdams, Reynolds, Lewis, Patten
&  Bowman,  2001).  Additionally,  life  stories  are  psychological  constructions,  developed  by
the individual and cultural context within which that person’s life is embedded (McAdams,
2001). Hence, life stories reflect cultural norms  and values; including beliefs about  gender,

[PDF page 23]
race  and  class.  As  will  be  elaborated  below,  life  stories  and  their  (re)construction  are  also
extremely important for establishing the (narrative) identity.
A  life  story  consists  of  numerous  autobiographical  memories,  these  are  the  things
people remember during the course of the life. These memories emerge and develop in the
social  context,  bounded  in  time  (McAdams,  2001).  From  these  autobiographical  memories,
people encode, store and retrieve information for their life narratives or life stories, which is
also called autobiographical reasoning:

‘‘A process of self-reflective thinking or talking about the personal past that involves
forming links between elements of one’s life and the self in an attempt to relate one’s
personal  past  and  present.  It  relies  on  autobiographical  remembering,  but  it  goes
beyond  it  by  enhancing  understanding  through  actively  creating  coherence  between
events and the self.’’ (Habermas & Bluck, 2000, p. 749).

Most autobiographical memories can be seen as summarised events consisting of general or
blended  information  from  multiple  associated  autobiographical  episodes  (McAdams,  2001).
According to McAdams (in Pemberton, Aarten & Mulder, forthcoming), nuclear episodes are
of major importance within one’s life story. Nuclear episodes are autobiographical episodes of
a particular and enduring relevance. Memories of such episodes serve as an important script
for present and future behaviour, depending on the accomplishment of future, long-term goals
(Pemberton, Aarten & Mulder, forthcoming). The experience of severe forms of victimisation
is  an  example  of  a  nuclear  episode.  In  comparison  to  positive  life  events,  it  turns  out  that
negative life events, e.g. victimisation, play a key role within one’s life story. These negative
life  events  offer  the  storyteller  a  challenge;  it  demands  an  explanation  of  the  causes  of  the
event, the consequences and the further course of the life story.
The function of life stories or narratives, e.g. autobiographies, is to reveal structures or
meanings of events in life that were implicit or unrecognised before (Crossley, 2000). With an
eye on the theoretical notions concerning the life story and current research, the narratives of
the Afghan victims can teach us how they construct their life story, why they construct it in a
certain way and how they give meaning to their (negative) life events. It is likely to assume
that  the  life  stories  of  the  Afghan  victims  are  also  characterised  by  nuclear  episodes  about
their victimhood.

Narrative identity
An important issue is the role of life stories in the development and maintenance of identity
and personality. Telling life stories help individuals organise their recollective memories and

[PDF page 24]
the more abstract knowledge they have of their past life (Habermas & Bluck, 2000). This is an
important way to create self-understanding and self-continuity. Out of the life story, people
construct and internalise certain aspects into a developing and integrative story for life, this is
also  called  the  narrative  identity  (McAdams  &  McLean,  2013).  The  narrative  identity
organises the autobiographical past and future perspectives in such a way that it provides an
individual a certain degree of unity, purpose and meaning. By means of the narrative identity,
people can tell who they are, how they came to be this way and how they see themselves in
the future. Since the narrative identity is such a fundamental aspect of one’s existence, it is
interesting to see if and how the experience of severe victimisation has threatened or changed
the narrative identity of the Afghan victims.
McLean,  Pasupathi  and  Pals  (2007,  in  McAdams  &  McLean,  2013)  developed  a
sociocultural  model  to  provide  insight  in  the  development  of  the  narrative  identity.  This
model clarifies that the narrative identity evolves slowly over time as people tell stories about
their  experiences  to  others,  and  with  others.  Over  this  developmental  time,  selves  create
stories,  which  in  turn  create  selves  (McAdams  &  McLean,  2013).  People  reconstruct  their
internalised narratives of the self to address on-time and off-time changes in life (McAdams et
al.,  2001).  Through  recurring  interactions  with  other  people,  stories  about  personal  events
become  processed,  edited,  reinterpreted,  retold  and  subjected  to  different  kinds  of  (social)
influences. As a result, an individual eventually develops a broader and integrative narrative
identity (McAdams & McLean, 2013). So, the establishment of a narrative identity by means
of the life story is a psychosocial construction (McAdams et al., 2001).
In view of the construction of the personality, McAdams (2013) developed the notion
of  the  threefold  psychological  self.  The  idea  behind  the  threefold  psychological  self  is  that
people  comprehend  themselves  from  three  different  psychological  standpoints:  the  self  as
actor, the self as agent and the self as author. The self as actor entails traits, social roles and
other aspects of the self that are developed by repeated performances and interactions on the
social stage of life (McAdams, 2013). The self as motivated agent refers to the goals, motives,
values, hopes and fears and other features that relate to major decisions and choices a person
has to make with regards to exploration of and commitment to life projects (McAdams, 2013).
Finally,  the  self  as  autobiographical  author,  which  considers  the  self  as  a  storyteller  who
intends to incorporate episodic information into a coherent life story (McAdams, 2013). Here
is where the narrative identity appears to be important. The self as author tries to achieve self-
continuity; the self of today is the same as the self of yesterday and tomorrow (Pemberton,
Aarten & Mulder, forthcoming). Every human being starts his or her life as a social actor and

[PDF page 25]
slowly evolves over time into the self as agent and later during the late adolescence to the self
as author.
The development of the narrative identity and the self is in conjunction with the wider
narrative of the  group or culture  an individual belongs to or lives in. The link between the
narrative identity  and the culture an individual lives in seems to be dual. On the one hand,
culture provides the narrative scripts that human beings use to frame their own life story. On
the other hand, culture is the means by which individuals incorporate their own experiences
within  the  wider  society  or  culture  (McAdams  and  Pals,  2006,  Hammack,  2008,  in
Pemberton, Aarten & Mulder, forthcoming).

Sense and meaning making
Humans  are  meaning-making  creatures  and  make  sense  of  their  life  experiences.  Through
story-telling,  people  attach  meaning  to  life  experiences  (Crossley,  2000).  Victimisations
affects  and  changes  an  individual’s  assumptions  about  meaning-making;  it  challenges  an
individual  to  re-establish  a  sense  of  meaning  within  life  (Crossley  2000;  Janoff-Bulman,
2004).  With  this  in  mind,  present  research  sheds  light  on  the  sense-  and  meaning-making
process  of  the  Afghan  victims  who  all  experienced  different  forms  of  severe  victimisation.

According to Janoff-Bulman (2004), there are two types of meaning-making. The first
type  of  meaning-making  is  ‘meaning  as  comprehensibility’,  which  refers  to  the  notion  that
victims in the immediate aftermath of victimisation are mainly concerned with questions of
comprehensibility; they have problems with making sense of the traumatic event. The second
type of meaning-making is ‘meaning of significance’. As a consequence of the struggle with
the  question  of  comprehensibility,  victims  become  entangled  in  the  question  of  value  or
significance in their lives (Janoff-Bulman, 2004).
Especially severe forms of victimisation challenge the process of sense and meaning
making. This might cause difficulties chiefly because these episodes of victimisation play a
major part in someone’s life story. Besides the fact that the experience of victimisation affects
a victim’s self-esteem and sense of self-control, it brings along a narrative challenge as well
(Brody, 1987, in Pemberton, Aarten & Mulder, forthcoming). People have main assumptions
and beliefs about the world as a virtuous place, but when victimisation comes in, these main
assumptions  about  the  world  become  disturbed  and  damaged.  This  is  also  called  shattered
assumptions (Janoff-Bulman, in Pemberton, Aarten & Mulder, forthcoming). As a result, the
victimisation might cause a rupture between the experience of the self before, during and after

[PDF page 26]
the victimisation (Pemberton, Aarten & Mulder, forthcoming).
However,  it  goes  further  than  that:  the  shattered  assumptions  can  induce a  narrative
rupture.  The  experience  of  victimisation  and  traumatic  life  events  disrupts  an  individual’s
routine  and  orderly  sense  of  existence  and  it  questions  the  taken-for-granted  assumptions
about  time,  identity,  meaning  and  life  itself  (Crossley,  2000).  In  that  case  the  shattered
assumptions  entangle  the  victim’s  sense  of  self-continuity  and  the  sense  of  continuity  with
others (Pemberton, Aarten & Mulder, forthcoming). In other words, a traumatised individual
often suffers from a lack of connection and continuity within his or her own life story; the
lack of connection and continuity between the past, present and future. At the same time, the
connection and sense of belonging with the social environment of the victim is threatened. In
the  long  term,  somehow,  the  victimisation  experience  needs  to  be  accommodated  or
assimilated  within  one’s  story.  Nevertheless,  the  self  of  victims  is  changed  in  one  way  or
another.

Analysing the narratives
With  regards  to  the  narrative  perspective,  Polkinghorne  (1995)  speaks  of  narrative
configuration.  This  is  the  process  whereby  events  are  assembled  and  integrated  into  a
temporally integrated whole:

‘’This configuration process employs a thematic threat to lay out happenings as parts
of an unfolding movement that culminates in an outcome. The thematic threat is  called
the plot, and the plot’s integrating operation is called emplotment. When  happenings
are  configured  or  emplotted,  they  take  on  narrative  meaning.  That  is,  they  are
understood from the perspective of their contribution and influence on a  specified
outcome.’’ (Polkinghorne, 1995, p. 1.)

In line with the configuration process, Polkinghorne (1995) argues that there are two types of
narrative  inquiry,  i.e.  two  ways  to  analyse  narratives.  The  first  type  is  called  ‘analysis  of
narratives’. Shortly said, this type of analysis aims to find in an inductive and paradigmatic
way common elements derived from different stories. Such a paradigmatic analysis results in
a comprehensive description of themes that apply to the stories or to taxonomies of types of
stories,  characters  and  settings.  The  analysis  goes  further  than  simply  discovering  common
themes and elements derived from the data. It ultimately intends to effectuate a second level
of  analysis,  which  means  that  there  will  be  sought  for  relationships  and  links  that  hold
between and among the discovered themes and elements (Polkinghorne, 1995). In order to be
able to find themes and underlying relationships, it is necessary to zoom in on the narratives.

[PDF page 27]
The second type of analysis is called the ‘narrative analysis’. This analysis focuses on
composing the different data elements into a united plot which gives meaning to the data as
contributors  to  a  goal  or  purpose  (Polkinghorne,  1995).  The  task  of  the  researcher  is  to
develop or discover a plot that represents the connection among the different data elements.
This plot needs to fit the data while at the same time it needs to shed light on new elements
and meanings that do not appear in the data themselves. The aim of this analysis is to discover
how and why a certain outcome occurred (Polkinghorne, 1995). In order to be able to discover
or develop an overarching plotline of the narratives, it is necessary to zoom out and look at
the narratives from a distance.
In order to obtain a full picture of the narratives of the Afghan victims, the twofold
analysis  as  described  above  is  also  useful  for  current  research.  Therefore,  in  line  with  the
ideas of Polkinghorne (1995), the text below first discusses the main themes in human life, the
so  called  ‘zoom  in’.  With  these  main  themes  in  mind,  the  ‘analysis  of  narratives’  can  be
conducted at a later stage of current research. Subsequently, the different plotlines in human
life will be discussed, the so called ‘zoom out’. These plotlines need to be taken into account
in current research during the ‘narrative analysis’ of the life stories of the Afghan victims.

Zooming in: important themes in life
Redemption and contamination
In light of this research, it is especially important how individuals make sense of the suffering
and traumatic experiences in their lives. The common themes redemption and contamination
seem to be important in this meaning-making process. Therefore both themes are included in
this  theoretical  framework.  It  is  interesting  to  find  out  in  current  research  how  the  Afghan
victims make sense of their victimhood in terms of redemption and contamination.
As  can  be  read  above,  there  are  two  types  of  sense-  and  meaning-making  after  a
victimisation  experience.  The  question  is  what  victims  do  after  the  sense-  and  meaning-
making process. Research on the earlier mentioned narrative identity shows that adults who
turned  out  to  be  strengthened  from  negative  life  events  often  engage  in  a  two-step  process
(McAdams & McLean, 2013). The first step is the process of thinking long and deeply about
what the event felt like, how it came to be, what the result might be and what kind of role the
negative experience might have in the general life story. During the second step, an individual
commits the self to a positive resolution of the experience (McAdams & McLean, 2013). This
kind of self-exploration often provides life lessons and insights that enrich a person’s life in
the long term, this is called the redemption sequence. So, when an individual experiences a

[PDF page 28]
negative  and  traumatic  life  event,  which  causes  pain  and  suffering,  (s)he  will  believe  that
something good will soon happen. Research on this redemption sequence shows that people
who perceive benefits in adversity seem to have a better recovery from and adjustment to the
traumatic event that brought them pain and suffering at first (McAdams et al., 2001). People
who  overcome  their  trauma  tend  to  have  an  increased  self-reliance  and  self-understanding,
improved  self-disclosure  and  emotional  expressiveness  in  relationships  and  an  altered  life
philosophy (McAdams et al., 2001).
By  contrast,  there  is  the  contamination  sequence.  In  case  of  contamination,  an
individual transforms a good and positive life event into a bad and negative life event. The
positive  event  is  destroyed,  spoiled,  contaminated  or  overshadowed  by  what  followed
(McAdams et al., 2001). An individual might try to return to the positive life event and its
corresponding mind-set, but this is often doomed to failure.

Agency and communion
The  shattered  assumptions,  as  explained  above,  not  only  cause  a  narrative  rupture,  it  also
menaces two of the most common and important themes in the life stories of human beings:
agency and communion (McAdams, Hoffman, Mansfield & Day, 1996). Both themes provide
consistency within an individual’s life story and are therefore important (Bauer, McAdams &
Pals, 2006). Besides, these two concepts are used by the individual to indicate their relation to
their  social  world  (Diehl,  Owen  &  Youngblade,  2004).  The  concepts  of  agency  and
communion  are  related  to  psychological  processes.  It  refers  to  an  individual’s  style  of
reasoning,  social  status  evaluations,  personality  traits,  sex-role  socialisation  and  the  self-
concept (Diehl, Owen & Youngblade, 2004).
Almost all autobiographical narratives contain agency elements. Shortly said: agency
is  about  the  existence  of  the  organism  as  an  individual.  It  refers  to  an  individual’s  goal  to
master  the  environment,  to  assert  the  self  and  to  experience  competence,  achievement  and
power (Diehl, Owen & Youngblade, 2004). So when an individual is telling a story about an
important experience of the self, several agency concepts can be noticed: self-mastery, status,
achievement/responsibility and empowerment (McAdams et al., 1996). When an individual is
agency-oriented,  (s)he  is  satisfied  when  (s)he  experiences  personal  successes  and
accomplishments  and  when  (s)he  gains  a  feeling  of  independency  and  separateness  (Diehl,
Owen & Youngblade, 2004).
The same thing can be said about communion and the importance of this theme within
human life. The concept of communion refers to the participation of an individual in a larger

[PDF page 29]
organism of which the individual is a part (McAdams et al., 1996). Even though less attention
is  paid  to  the  concept  of  communion,  it  is  equally  important  as  the  concept  of  agency.
Communion points out an individual’s devotion to closely relate to and cooperate and merge
with  others  (Diehl,  Owen  &  Youngblade,  2014).  The  core  of  communion  is  that  different
people come together in loving, close and communicative relationships. Communion concepts
within someone´s life story are: love/friendship, dialogue, care/help and community. In case
of  communion-oriented  individuals,  (s)he  feels  satisfaction  by  their  sense  of  belonging  and
the relationships with other people (Diehl, Owen & Youngblade, 2004).
The  experience  of  victimisation  poses  a  threat  to  both  themes.  In  the  first  place,
experiencing a traumatic life event calls into question agentic competence (Pemberton, Aarten
&  Mulder,  forthcoming).  It  reduces  the  victim’s  feeling  of  self-control,  self-esteem  and
respect. Since agency is a main theme in human life, current research tries to discover what
the experience of severe victimisation has done to the sense of agency of the Afghan victims.
Based on the theoretical notions, it is assumable that the severe victimisation has adversely
affected this theme in life. At the same time, severe victimisation threatens the victim’s sense
of  communion.  Due  to  victimisation,  a  victim  might  doubt  his  values  and  morality  shared
with his or her community, that the offender is also a part of (Pemberton, Aarten & Mulder,
forthcoming). This in turn affects the sense of togetherness the victim experiences as part of
his or her community. With an eye on the situation of the Afghan victims, it therefore seems
to  be  painful  to  be  confronted  again  with  their  offenders  in  the  Netherlands.  The  Afghan
victims fled from the community their offenders were part of, yet these offenders are part of
the same community in the Netherlands. This possibly impedes the process of re-establishing
their sense of community.
When  both  fundamental  life  themes  are  affected  through  severe  victimisation,  it
possibly causes a sense of dehumanisation and it might stimulate the loss of connection to the
rest  of  humanity  (Pemberton,  Aarten  &  Mulder,  forthcoming).  After  an  experience  of
victimisation,  victims  often  feel  the  motivation  to  re-establish  their  sense  of  agency  and
communion. This can be done, as explained above, by means of sense- and meaning-making
processes  and  the  redemption  sequence.  The  victimisation  experience  has  affected  the
victims’  main  assumptions  about  life  which  in  turn  influences  the  sense  and  meaning  they
attach to their (future) life events. The main assumptions they once had need to be repaired in
order to be able to re-establish their sense of agency and communion. Once the experience of
victimisation is assimilated in an adequate way within the life story, victims might be able to

[PDF page 30]
be strengthened from the victimisation experience which might lead to the re-establishment of
their sense of agency and communion.

Zooming out: plotlines
Stories  can  be  seen  as  the  linguistic  form  in  which  human  life  as  lived  can  be  expressed
(Polkinghorne, 1995). In a life story, life experiences and events are taken together by means
of  a  plot.  However,  the  remarkable  thing  of  (life)  stories  is  that  whoever  tells  the  story,
wherever in the world, the stories seem to follow similar plots. There seems to be recurring
themes and situations all individuals include in their stories (Booker, 2004). The similarity of
stories appears in the way of telling: in the use of characters, their point of view, suspense and
so on (Polletta, 2009). At the same time, the audiences that listen to the stories have certain
expectations in line with other, familiar stories.
Booker (2004) believed that there are seven universal and basic stories or plotlines that
individuals refer to during story telling. People make sense of their world by framing events
and sentences in a larger structure, also called a plot. A plot is a narrative structure through
which people comprehend and outline the relation between events and choices of their lives
(Bruner in Polkinghorne, 1995). A plot has several functions within a (life) story. First of all,
a  plot  determines  the  beginning  and  the  end  of  a  story,  so  it  provides  a  temporal  range.
Secondly, it offers several criteria for which events and choices will be included in the story.
Moreover,  a  plot  orders  different  events  into  a  temporary  whole  which  will  culminate  in  a
conclusion. And finally, a plot clarifies the meaning of the different events in life and makes
explicit  in  which  way  the  events  contribute  to  the  story  as  a  united  whole  (Bruner  in
Polkinghorne, 1995).
The  first  plotline  that  can  be  distinguished  according  to  Booker  (2004)  is  called:
‘Overcoming the Monster’. Basically, within this story the hero must confront a powerful and
horrible monster in a fight to the death. The monster can be in the form of a human being, an
animal or a combination of both and often possesses something the hero wanted to have or
save,  such  as  a  princess  or  another  treasure.  In  the  end,  the  hero  wins  the  fight  with  the
monster and gets a valuable reward. This kind of story is remarked by a long build-up and a
climax at the end of the story.
The second plot line that can be distinguished is called: ‘Rags to Riches’. This story is
about  a  young,  unrecognized  hero  or  heroine  who  is  lifted  out  of  obscurity,  poverty  and
misery to a state of greatness and happiness (Booker, 2004). However, this upgrade is not a
continuous unbroken climb. The unfortunate main character has to overcome many things in

[PDF page 31]
life in order to achieve the ‘riches’.
The third plotline that can be differentiated is called: ‘Quest’. In quest stories there is
one  ultimate,  priceless  life  goal  that  the  main  character  wants  to  achieve,  for  example
promised land or freedom. Reaching this goal becomes the most important thing in life and
the main character will do anything in his power to achieve the goal (Booker, 20014). Another
noteworthy aspect of quest stories is that the main character, the hero, is often accompanied
by friends who help accomplish this goal. The story comes to an end when the ultimate aim
has finally been reached.
The fourth plotline that can be mentioned is: ‘Voyage and Return’. This story entails a
journey  as  well,  but  it  differs  from  the  quest  story  in  several  ways  (Booker,  2004).  In  this
story  the  hero  or  heroine  travels  out  of  their  familiar  everyday  world  into  a  completely
different  world  cut  off  from  the  first.  The  new  world  consists  of  abnormal  and  strange
elements which astonish and inspire the hero/heroine at first. Gradually a dark side appears
and the hero or heroine feels uncomfortable in the new world. Eventually (usually as a result
of a thrilling scene) the hero or heroine escapes from the abnormal world and returns to their
normal world (Booker, 2004). The journey to the ‘other’ world changes the hero or heroine in
a positive way; there is a deeper understanding of the world.
Additionally, the fifth plot line that can be named is ‘Comedy’. This story is a very
specific kind of story and not just a ‘funny story’. The plots of comedy stories vary, but they
do have some similarities (Booker, 2004). Generally, a comedy story is about a small world in
which people have passed under a shadow of confusion, uncertainty and frustration, and are
shut off from one another. The confusion becomes worse until the pressure of darkness is at
its peak making people’s lives a nightmare. Finally, people start to recognise things they did
not see before and therefore their perceptions about life changes. The result is a transformed,
united small world where people live together joyfully (Booker, 2004). So, the main subject
of comedy stories is the transition between two states.
The sixth plotline is called: ‘Tragedy’. These stories have a tragic and sad theme and,
in contrast to the other plotlines, no happy ending. Basically these stories show the lives of
human beings who are caught up in a course of (negative) actions which will eventually result
in a violent and unnatural death (Booker, 2004).
The last and seventh plotline that can be mentioned is called: ‘Rebirth’. Just like the
other plotlines, the rebirth plotline has something unique (Booker, 2004). Commonly, a hero
deals with a dark power in his life and gets poisoned by this dark power. As a result, the hero
gets isolated which is a disaster for the hero and his loved ones. In the end, the hero is freed

[PDF page 32]
by the power of love (Booker, 2004). Similar to other plotlines, the hero switches from a dark
to a light world.
Back in 1957, Frye noted another plotline, called ‘Irony’. The best way to describe this
plotline is as following: ‘’We encounter ambiguities in life that are larger than we are and that
are, for the most part, beyond our comprehension.’’ (Frye, p.52, in Sandage, 2012). It often
involves  the  mockery  of  conventional  values  and  standards,  without  the  intention  to  hurt
someone. Often these stories are tragic and ironic at the same time (Sandage, 2012).
What can be learned from these plotlines is that all individuals, probably unknowingly,
make  use  of  a  certain  plotline  while  telling  their  (life)  stories.  The  way  victims  choose  a
plotline  for  the  representation  of  their  life  story  might  be  relevant.  The  plotline  might  say
something about the way the victims perceive their life story, their role within this life story
and how they deal with the things that have happened to them. Moreover, in light of current
research, it is interesting to notice that all plotlines, with the exception of the comedy plotline,
include  a  victim  role.  Therefore  it  seems  useful  to  compare  the  narratives  of  the  Afghan
victims and its (unconsciously) chosen plots with the plotlines as conceived by Booker and
Frye. However, it is important to notice that although all individuals seem to pick a plotline
while telling stories, it is not likely that real life stories fit perfectly into one specific plotline.
Especially  (auto)biographies  often  correspond  partially  to  a  single  plotline  (Polkinghorne,
1995). This has to be taken into account while examining narratives.

Current research
This  chapter  served  as  a  theoretical  background.  Current  research  aims  to  make  a  linkage
between  the  foregoing  chapters:  the  Afghan  history,  the  theory  concerning  the  narrative
perspective and the Afghan victims’ narratives. With the Afghan history and its narratives in
mind, and the theoretical notions above taken into account, the gathered Afghan narratives of
current research can be analysed in a meaningful and comprehensive way.
